Including that height in the area calculation would measure a different face or a three-dimensional quantity. Identify the plane's orientation before selecting dimensions.

### Example 2: A square pyramid

A square pyramid has a square base and an apex above its center. A plane parallel to the base, between the base and apex, produces a smaller square. Moving the plane toward the apex makes the section smaller. Moving it toward the base makes the section larger, approaching the base square.

A plane passing through the apex and the midpoint of two opposite base edges instead creates a triangular section. This is a different orientation and therefore a different shape. The phrase “a pyramid is sliced” does not identify which of these occurs. The cutting plane must be described in relation to the base and apex.

## Read a section diagram systematically

First name the solid and identify its base or relevant face. Next locate the cutting plane: parallel to a face, perpendicular to a base, or at another angle. Then trace the intersection around the faces. The section's vertices lie where the plane meets edges, and its sides lie along the plane's intersections with faces.

Do not count hidden edges of the original solid as section sides unless the cutting plane actually follows them. Dashed lines in a perspective diagram may indicate hidden solid edges or construction lines, so read the caption. A section polygon must close around the cut without jumping to an unrelated edge.

## Practice predicting and checking

For a box with dimensions six by four by three, identify the section parallel to the six-by-four base: a six-by-four rectangle. Its area is twenty-four square units. Now identify a section parallel to a four-by-three side face: a four-by-three rectangle with area twelve. Both are rectangular, but they use different dimensions.

A cube has side length five. Every interior section parallel to a face is a five-by-five square. A corner-cutting plane can instead make a triangle. This contrast shows that knowing all faces are squares does not force all cross-sections to be squares. The orientation of the plane supplies essential information.

Draw a square pyramid and sketch two parallel planes at different heights below its apex. Label their cross-sections as squares, with the higher one smaller. You do not need to estimate exact side lengths unless the problem supplies enough scale information. Shape can be determined even when exact dimensions are not known.

Now describe a slice through the apex and a base diagonal of the square pyramid. The section is a triangle whose base lies along that diagonal. Its base length is not the same as one base edge. Avoid inventing a diagonal measurement from a schematic picture; leave dimensions unspecified unless they are given or can be justified by methods already established.

## Common mistakes

A view from outside is not a cross-section. Perspective can make a rectangle appear slanted, so use geometric relationships rather than screen angles. A prism's height is not automatically a section dimension. Finally, sections of a pyramid parallel to its base shrink toward the apex, while corresponding sections of a prism retain their size.

## Key points

- A cross-section is the intersection of a plane and a solid.
- Shape and size depend on the cutting plane.
- Face-parallel rectangular-prism sections match that face.
- Base-parallel pyramid sections are smaller copies of the base.
- Trace the intersection and state its conditions before naming the shape.

lessons.title: Find volumes of right prisms
lessons.body:
## Volume counts three-dimensional space

A storage box holds layers of objects, not just a covering of one face. **[[Volume]]** measures the three-dimensional space occupied or enclosed by a solid. A **[[cubic unit]]** is the volume of a cube with edge length one unit. A **[[base area]]** is the area of a chosen base face or region. The **[[perpendicular height]]** of a prism is the shortest distance between its parallel bases.

For a right prism, volume is $V=Bh$, where $B$ is base area and $h$ is perpendicular height. The formula counts repeated layers of the same cross-section. It works for rectangular and triangular bases and other polygonal bases, provided the solid is a prism with congruent parallel bases and the height is chosen correctly.

## Connect layers to the formula

A box with base four units by three units has room for twelve unit cubes in one layer. If it is five units high, five layers contain sixty cubes. Thus $V=(4\cdot3)\cdot5=60$ cubic units. The familiar rectangular-prism formula $lwh$ is the same as $Bh$ with $B=lw$.

![A rectangular-prism volume can be interpreted as repeated equal layers.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A rectangular-prism volume can be interpreted as repeated equal layers.

Fractional dimensions also fit the layer model. Imagine subdividing unit cubes into smaller equal cubes so that a half-unit or quarter-unit dimension can be represented. The number of smaller cubes and the volume of each combine to give the same multiplication rule. A noninteger volume is not a contradiction; the solid may occupy a fraction of a cubic unit.

Keep base area and a base edge distinct. If a triangular base has area six square centimeters and the prism is ten centimeters long, volume is sixty cubic centimeters. Multiplying a single triangle edge by ten would miss the other dimension needed to find the base area. The capital $B$ in the formula stands for an area, not just a length named “base.”

## Triangular-prism volume

A triangle's area is half its base edge times its perpendicular altitude: $B=\frac12ba$. For a right triangular prism, multiply that triangular area by the distance between the two triangular bases. There are two different heights to track: the altitude inside the triangle and the prism's height or length between the bases.

For example, a triangular base with base edge eight and perpendicular altitude three has area twelve. If the prism extends seven units between congruent triangular ends, its volume is $12\cdot7=84$ cubic units. Label the dimensions before calculating so the triangle's altitude is not confused with the prism length.

### Example 1: A rectangular prism with fractions

A rectangular container has inside dimensions $2\frac12$ meters, $1\frac12$ meters, and $\frac45$ meter. Its capacity in cubic meters is $\frac52\cdot\frac32\cdot\frac45=3$. Simplify factors before multiplying or calculate $2.5\cdot1.5\cdot0.8=3$.

The use of inside dimensions matters because capacity refers to the space available within the walls. Outside dimensions would include wall thickness unless that thickness were negligible under the model. The answer is three cubic meters, not three square meters. Check the units: meters times meters times meters gives cubic meters.

### Example 2: Find a missing prism height

A right prism has base area eighteen square centimeters and volume one hundred twenty-six cubic centimeters. Find its perpendicular height. From $V=Bh$, write $126=18h$. Dividing by eighteen gives $h=7$ centimeters.

Check by rebuilding the volume: eighteen square centimeters per one-centimeter layer times seven centimeters gives one hundred twenty-six cubic centimeters. Dividing volume by area leaves a length unit. An answer in square centimeters would indicate that the calculation's meaning was not interpreted correctly, even if the number seven were obtained.

## Use consistent units

Convert all length dimensions to compatible units before multiplying, or convert areas and volumes with the correct powers. A box measuring fifty centimeters by forty centimeters by thirty centimeters has volume sixty thousand cubic centimeters. In meters, its dimensions are $0.5$, $0.4$, and $0.3$, giving $0.06$ cubic meter.

One meter is one hundred centimeters, but one cubic meter contains $100^3=1{,}000{,}000$ cubic centimeters. Multiplying a volume conversion by only one hundred would confuse a length factor with a three-dimensional factor. You can avoid this mistake by converting each length first, then multiplying.

## Practice choosing the base

A prism has a rectangular face three by five and extends eight units perpendicular to that face. Its volume is fifteen times eight, or one hundred twenty cubic units. You could choose a different rectangular face as the base and still obtain the same product of three dimensions. The chosen base and height must remain perpendicular partners.

A triangular prism has triangular base edge six centimeters, triangle altitude four centimeters, and prism length nine centimeters. The base area is twelve square centimeters, and volume is one hundred eight cubic centimeters. Explain why multiplying six, four, and nine without the one-half factor would double the volume.

A prism's base area is $7.5$ square meters and its height is $2.4$ meters. Volume is eighteen cubic meters. Estimate first: about eight times about two is around sixteen, so eighteen is plausible. If the calculation produced one hundred eighty, a decimal-place error would be likely.

A box's volume is ninety-six cubic units, with length eight and width four. Its base area is thirty-two, so its height is three. Substitute all three dimensions into $lwh$ to verify. There are many other triples with volume ninety-six, but the two given dimensions determine the third in this model.

## Common mistakes

Do not use a slanted edge as a perpendicular height unless it is actually perpendicular to the base. Do not omit the one-half factor for a triangular base. Distinguish volume from surface area, and convert units using powers appropriate to the measurement. Finally, decide whether the task concerns inside capacity or outside occupied space.

## Key points

- A right prism's volume is base area times perpendicular height.
- Calculate the base area before multiplying by prism height.
- Track separate triangle and prism heights when needed.
- Use cubic units for volume.
- Check missing dimensions by reconstructing the original volume.

lessons.title: Use nets to find surface area
topics: Use nets to find surface area
lessons.body:
## Surface area measures the covering

Wrapping a box requires material for its faces, while filling the box concerns its volume. **[[Surface area]]** is the total area of the surfaces included in a task. A **[[net]]** is a flat arrangement of faces that can fold into a solid without overlap. A **[[lateral face]]** is a side face connecting a prism's bases. A **[[slant height]]** of a regular pyramid is the perpendicular altitude within one of its triangular side faces.

Specify which surfaces are included. A closed box has six faces; an open-top container omits its top from the material calculation. A solid sitting on a table may still have a bottom surface, even if you cannot see it. Whether that bottom needs paint or wrapping depends on the question, not merely on the viewpoint of the drawing.

## Use a net as an inventory

A rectangular prism with length $l$, width $w$, and height $h$ has two faces of area $lw$, two of area $lh$, and two of area $wh$. Its total closed surface area is $2lw+2lh+2wh$. This formula summarizes the face list. Building the list first is a reliable way to avoid missing a face or using a length where an area belongs.

![This valid box net contains four three-by-two rectangles and two two-by-two squares.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This valid box net contains four three-by-two rectangles and two two-by-two squares.

In the net, opposite faces have matching dimensions. The side strip wraps around the base, and the other two rectangles close the ends. Not every collection of six rectangles is a valid net; the edges must meet appropriately when folded, and faces must not overlap. A net is a geometric arrangement, not just a list of areas.

Surface area uses square units. Multiplying three dimensions gives volume, which uses cubic units and answers a different question. A box can have a large surface area relative to its volume if it is long and thin. There is no single universal number that converts volume into surface area without information about shape and dimensions.

## Triangular-prism faces

A right triangular prism has two congruent triangular bases and three rectangular lateral faces. First calculate one triangle's area, then double it. Each lateral rectangle has one side equal to a triangle edge and the other equal to the prism length. Adding those three rectangles gives the triangle's perimeter times the prism length.

Thus a right prism's lateral area can be written as base perimeter times prism height. Total surface area adds the two base areas. This method works because the lateral faces are rectangles in a right prism. Keep base perimeter and base area distinct: one contributes to the side strip, while the other contributes to the two ends.

### Example 1: A closed rectangular box

A closed rectangular box measures eight centimeters by five centimeters by three centimeters. The two large faces each have area forty square centimeters, the two long side faces each have area twenty-four, and the two short side faces each have area fifteen. Total surface area is $2(40)+2(24)+2(15)=158$ square centimeters.

Its volume is $8\cdot5\cdot3=120$ cubic centimeters. These numbers measure different features. If the box had no top, remove one forty-square-centimeter face from the surface calculation, leaving one hundred eighteen square centimeters. Do not remove both large faces unless the task states that both top and bottom are absent.

### Example 2: A right triangular prism

A prism has right-triangle bases with perpendicular legs three and four centimeters and hypotenuse five centimeters. The prism length is ten centimeters. One triangular base has area $\frac12(3)(4)=6$ square centimeters, so both bases contribute twelve.

The lateral faces have areas thirty, forty, and fifty square centimeters. Their sum is one hundred twenty, and total surface area is one hundred thirty-two square centimeters. The perimeter shortcut gives $(3+4+5)(10)=120$ for the lateral area, confirming the same result. The five-centimeter hypotenuse is a rectangle width, not the triangle's perpendicular altitude when using base three or four.

## Pyramid surface area

A square pyramid has one square base and four triangular side faces. If each base edge is six centimeters and every side face has slant height five centimeters, the base area is thirty-six and each side triangle's area is $\frac12(6)(5)=15$. Total surface area is $36+4(15)=96$ square centimeters.

The slant height lies in a triangular face and is perpendicular to that face's base edge. The pyramid's vertical height goes from apex toward the base plane and is a different segment. Do not substitute vertical height into the side-triangle area formula unless the task explicitly establishes that it is the needed face altitude. A diagram should label which height is supplied.

## Practice counting included faces

A cube has side length four meters. Each square face has area sixteen square meters, and all six contribute ninety-six square meters. Its volume is sixty-four cubic meters. If only five faces are painted, the painted area is eighty square meters. State the included-face assumption before multiplying.

An open-top rectangular tray has inside dimensions six by four by two units, and the idealized task ignores material thickness. Its base area is twenty-four. The two long walls contribute twenty-four in total, and the two short walls contribute sixteen, giving sixty-four square units of interior surface. A closed-box formula would include an extra twenty-four for a top that is not present.

A right triangular prism has base area ten square units, base perimeter sixteen units, and prism length seven units. Its surface area is $2(10)+16(7)=132$ square units. The supplied base area already includes whatever triangle-area calculation was needed, so do not halve it again.

## Check a proposed net

Sketch a strip of four side rectangles for a box, alternating widths equal to the box's length and width. Attach a matching base and top at appropriate edges. Imagine folding each side upward and closing the top. Check edge lengths and whether any faces collide or leave a gap. You can use scrap paper for a physical model; the purpose is to connect the flat area inventory with the solid's actual surfaces.

## Common mistakes

Surface area counts faces, not edges. Do not use volume's three-factor formula. Keep triangular area heights perpendicular within their faces. Include or omit a top, bottom, or shared face according to the task, and do not assume an unseen face is absent.

## Key points

- List the surfaces that need covering.
- Use a net or face table to count each included face once.
- Right-prism lateral area is base perimeter times prism height.
- Add two base areas for a closed prism.
- Pyramid side areas require face altitudes, often called slant heights.

lessons.title: Measure composite solids and scale effects
topics: Measure composite solids and scale effects
lessons.body:
## Combine volumes without counting overlap twice

A stepped block can be built from two rectangular prisms, and a hollow object can be modeled by removing one prism from another. A **[[composite solid]]** combines simpler solids. **[[Nonoverlapping solids]]** have interiors that do not occupy the same space, although they may share a face. A **[[shared face]]** is a contact surface between joined pieces. A **[[volume scale factor]]** describes how volume changes under a uniform change of every length.

Volume can be added when pieces have nonoverlapping interiors. If pieces overlap, simply adding their volumes counts the overlapping space twice. If a cavity is removed from a larger solid, subtract the cavity's volume. State whether dimensions describe the remaining material, the whole bounding object, or the empty space, because these are different requested quantities.

## Decompose a stepped block

Imagine a lower rectangular prism six units long, four units wide, and two units high. A smaller prism three units long, four units wide, and one unit high sits on half its top. The lower volume is $6\cdot4\cdot2=48$, and the upper volume is $3\cdot4\cdot1=12$. Their interiors do not overlap, so the combined volume is sixty cubic units.

![The same stacked block uses addition for volume and a shared-face correction for exposed surface area.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The same stacked block uses addition for volume and a shared-face correction for exposed surface area.

The upper prism's height is only the extra one unit above the lower block. Using the total height three for the upper piece would count the space below it again. Mark the decomposition boundary before assigning dimensions. A labeled side view can help distinguish the height of one component from the height of the entire stack.

You could also start with a full six-by-four-by-three bounding prism and subtract the missing three-by-four-by-one region. That gives $72-12=60$ cubic units. Agreement between two valid decompositions is a strong arithmetic and coverage check. The methods must describe the same occupied region, not merely produce the same convenient number.

## Surface area requires contact accounting

The surface areas of joined solids cannot usually be added directly to find the exposed surface area. Each shared contact face appears once in each individual solid's surface area, but neither copy is exposed after joining. Subtract twice the contact area from the sum, provided there are no other overlaps or contacts to account for.

For the stepped block, the lower prism's surface area is $2(24+12+8)=88$. The upper prism's surface area is $2(12+3+4)=38$. Their contact area is twelve. The exposed surface area is $88+38-2(12)=102$ square units, including the bottom. Volume addition and surface-area adjustment use different reasoning because one counts occupied space and the other counts exposed faces.

### Example 1: Remove a rectangular cavity

An idealized block has outer dimensions ten by eight by six centimeters. A rectangular cavity four by three by two centimeters is removed from its top. Find the volume of material remaining. The original volume is $10\cdot8\cdot6=480$ cubic centimeters, and the removed volume is $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$. The remainder is $456$ cubic centimeters.

This calculation does not give the new surface area. Removing a cavity eliminates part of the old top but creates interior walls and a cavity floor. Surface area would need a separate inventory of the resulting exposed faces. A subtraction model that works for volume cannot automatically be copied for area without examining the surfaces.

### Example 2: Uniform enlargement

A rectangular prism measures two by three by four units. Its volume is twenty-four cubic units. Enlarge every length by a factor of three, giving dimensions six by nine by twelve. The new volume is $6\cdot9\cdot12=648$ cubic units, which is $27$ times twenty-four.

The factor twenty-seven is $3^3$ because all three length dimensions were multiplied by three. The surface-area factor is $3^2=9$, and a corresponding edge or perimeter factor is three. These three multipliers describe different measurements of the same enlargement. State which measurement you are scaling before applying a factor.

## Scaling one dimension is different

If only the height of a rectangular prism triples while length and width stay fixed, volume triples. It does not multiply by twenty-seven because only one factor changed. The new solid is not a uniform enlargement of the original; its shape proportions change. Surface area also does not use one universal factor in this one-dimension change because some faces change and others do not.

For a two-by-three-by-four prism, increasing only the height from four to twelve changes volume from twenty-four to seventy-two. The two base areas remain six each, while the side areas triple. Use the actual dimensions or face inventory to calculate the new surface area rather than applying a uniform scaling rule that does not fit.

## Practice choosing a decomposition

Join two cubes of side three along one full face. Their volumes add to $27+27=54$ cubic units. Their individual surface areas total $54+54=108$ square units, but the shared face has area nine and was counted twice. Exposed surface area is $108-18=90$ square units. Check by viewing the result as a six-by-three-by-three prism.

A five-by-five-by-four block has a two-by-two-by-four tunnel removed completely through it. The volume of material is $100-16=84$ cubic units. The tunnel creates inside boundary surfaces, so the remaining material's surface area needs more information and face accounting than simply subtracting the tunnel prism's full surface area.

A model is reduced with length factor one half. Its areas become one fourth as large, and its volumes become one eighth as large. If the original volume is sixty-four cubic units, the reduced volume is eight. Explain the three factors of one half by writing the product of scaled length, width, and height.

## State inclusion assumptions

For exposed surface area, specify whether the bottom counts, whether joined faces are fully in contact, and whether a cavity is open. For volume, specify whether the task asks for capacity, material, or the whole outer occupied region. The exercises use idealized exact dimensions and ignore wall thickness unless it is part of the given model. These assumptions keep the calculation tied to a clear geometric object.

## Common mistakes

Using total stack height for an upper component can double-count volume. Adding individual surface areas without removing contact faces overcounts exposed area. Applying a cubed factor when only one dimension changes confuses uniform scaling with stretching. Keep length, area, and volume units separate.

## Key points

- Add volumes of pieces with nonoverlapping interiors.
- Subtract a cavity's volume when finding remaining material.
- Remove shared faces twice from summed surface areas.
- Uniform length factor $s$ gives area factor $s^2$ and volume factor $s^3$.
- Check whether all dimensions or only selected dimensions change.

lessons.title: Design random samples
lessons.body:
## A sample should connect to a clear population

A school wants to know how students usually travel to school. Asking every student may take time, so it might survey a smaller group. The **[[population]]** is the complete group the question concerns. A **[[sample]]** is the subset actually observed or surveyed. A **[[representative sample]]** reflects relevant features of the population well enough to support the intended comparison. **[[Sampling bias]]** is a systematic tendency for a selection method to favor some parts of the population over others.

Define the population before choosing people. “Students at this school this term” differs from “all students in the district” or “families attending the evening event.” A sample can be useful for one of these groups and unsuitable for another. The conclusion should not quietly expand beyond the group the selection process could reasonably represent.

## Use a fair selection process

A simple random sample gives every possible group of the chosen size an equal chance of selection. One practical method is to number every student on a complete roster and select distinct numbers using a fair random process. Each student then has the same chance to be selected, and the method does not deliberately prefer a grade, activity, or friendship group.

![A random-sample plan separates selection from response and keeps the population explicit.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A random-sample plan separates selection from response and keeps the population explicit.

If selecting without replacement, a chosen student cannot be selected again for the same sample. If a random number repeats, follow the predetermined procedure, such as drawing another number until the required number of distinct students is reached. Do not replace a selected person with a convenient friend merely because that person is easier to reach; doing so changes the method.

Random selection improves the basis for inference but does not guarantee that one particular sample perfectly matches the population. By chance, a sample may contain more students from one grade or activity. Sampling variability remains even with a fair process. The important distinction is between chance variation and a method that systematically excludes or favors a group.

## Identify convenience and voluntary-response problems

Asking only students near the bicycle rack is convenient for a travel survey, but it is likely to overrepresent cyclists. Posting an optional online poll may overrepresent people with strong opinions or easy access to that platform. These methods can produce informative descriptions of respondents, but they need extra caution before describing the entire student population.

A very large biased sample does not automatically become representative. Surveying every person entering one sports event can still miss students who do not attend. Increasing the count reduces some random variation only when the selection process itself supports the intended inference. Size and selection quality are different considerations.

### Example 1: Compare two plans

A school of six hundred students wants to estimate preferred lunch options. Plan A asks fifty students in one advanced music class. Plan B randomly selects fifty distinct numbers from a current roster of all six hundred students. Plan B provides the stronger basis for a schoolwide estimate because every student can be selected through the same random procedure.

Plan A might accurately describe that class but may differ from the school in age, schedule, or interests. It is not necessary to prove that music students prefer different lunches to identify the concern. The selection method limits coverage and gives no reason to treat one class as a random cross-section of the school.

### Example 2: A fair draw with incomplete responses

A school randomly selects forty students, but only twenty return the survey. The initial selection was random; the final respondent group may not be representative if response is related to the question. For instance, students who strongly dislike the current schedule may be more motivated to reply.

Report that twenty of forty selected students responded. Follow a consistent, privacy-respecting reminder process if the study design allows it, and explain the remaining limitation. Do not claim that the twenty respondents are automatically a simple random sample just because the original forty were selected randomly. Selection and response are separate stages.

## Ask neutral, answerable questions

A fair sample cannot repair a leading question. “Do you agree that the wonderful new lunch menu is better?” pushes respondents toward a positive answer. A clearer question asks which menu they prefer and gives balanced choices, including an appropriate no-preference option when relevant. The wording should match what the study actually wants to measure.

Specify a time period for behavior questions. “How do you usually travel to school during this week?” is more precise than “How do you travel?” For a count, define what qualifies. If students count books read, clarify whether audiobooks and partially completed books are included. Consistent definitions make answers comparable.

## Practice reviewing sample plans

A library wants to estimate the fraction of all registered users who borrow audiobooks. Surveying only people in the audiobook section will overrepresent likely audiobook borrowers. A random sample from the full current user list is better aligned with the population. If users have different contact options, the plan should account for those differences rather than excluding everyone without email.

A teacher wants feedback about one particular class. Surveying every student in that class is a census of that class, not a sample of it. It still does not automatically describe other classes. The population definition determines whether an observed group is the whole population or a subset of a larger one.

A district samples one randomly chosen classroom and surveys everyone inside it. Every classroom may have an equal chance, but the resulting students are clustered together and may share characteristics. This is not the same as choosing the same number of individual students independently from a full roster. At this level, recognize the design difference and avoid calling every random-looking method a simple random sample.

## Plan an original study

Write a question about a non-sensitive school preference, define the population, and describe a complete selection list. Choose a sample size and explain the random procedure. Then identify a possible coverage or response problem and how you would report it. You do not need to collect personal data for this exercise; the goal is a reviewable plan with clear limitations.

## Common mistakes

Do not confuse a convenient group with a representative one. Random selection does not guarantee a perfect sample, and large size does not remove systematic bias. A response group can differ from the originally selected group. Finally, limit conclusions to the population the sampling design actually supports.

## Key points

- Define the population and question first.
- Use a complete, relevant selection list.
- Prefer a fair random procedure for population inference.
- Examine coverage, response, and question wording separately.
- Report limitations rather than treating a sample as a complete census.

lessons.title: Use samples to estimate population quantities
topics: Use samples to estimate population quantities
lessons.body:
## Use a sample as evidence, not as a complete count

Suppose a random sample of forty students includes fourteen who prefer a certain activity. The **[[sample proportion]]** is the observed count with that characteristic divided by the sample size: $14/40=0.35$. A **[[population estimate]]** uses sample information to approximate a quantity in the larger population. An **[[inference]]** is a conclusion extending beyond the observations directly collected. **[[Nonresponse]]** occurs when selected participants do not provide the requested information.

If the sample reasonably represents a school of six hundred students, an estimate of the number preferring the activity is $0.35(600)=210$. This is an estimate, not a verified count of two hundred ten particular students. The random sample gives evidence about the population while leaving uncertainty about unobserved members.

## Keep the numerator and denominator connected

The sample proportion must compare a subgroup count with the total observed sample count for the same question. If fourteen of forty respondents choose an activity, use fourteen divided by forty. Do not divide fourteen by the school population before estimating the population proportion. That would describe only the observed supporters as a share of the whole school, ignoring the unobserved students.

![A sample proportion projects a population count while retaining uncertainty about unobserved members.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A sample proportion projects a population count while retaining uncertainty about unobserved members.

A proportion can be expressed as a fraction, decimal, or percent. Fourteen fortieths reduces to seven twentieths, equals $0.35$, and represents thirty-five percent. These are equivalent forms of the same sample result. Choose the representation that makes the projection easy, keeping enough precision to avoid unnecessary rounding error.

The multiplication by population size assumes that the observed proportion is a reasonable stand-in for the population proportion. That assumption depends on the sampling design and response quality, not just on correct arithmetic. A biased sample can yield a precisely calculated but misleading estimate. Evaluate the evidence source before applying the proportion.

## State the direction of the inference

A sample drawn from one school supports an estimate for that school under the stated design. It does not automatically support an estimate for all schools. Likewise, a sample of current registered library users does not necessarily represent every resident in the town. The population used in the multiplication must match the population represented by the sample.

A statistical estimate also does not establish cause and effect. If students who attend a club report more reading, the sample may reveal an association, but it does not prove that the club caused the additional reading. Other differences could matter. Keep the inference at the level justified by the data and study design.

### Example 1: Estimate a population count

A random sample of sixty households from a neighborhood of nine hundred households includes eighteen with a compost bin. Assume all selected households respond and the roster covers the neighborhood. The sample proportion is $18/60=0.30$. The estimated number with a compost bin is $0.30(900)=270$ households.

Report “about two hundred seventy households, based on this sample.” The count could differ in the actual population. Check the arithmetic with a ratio: eighteen out of sixty is three out of ten, so roughly three out of every ten households are projected to have a bin. Three tenths of nine hundred is two hundred seventy.

### Example 2: A different sample gives a different estimate

Another independently selected random sample of sixty households includes twenty-one with a compost bin. Its sample proportion is $21/60=0.35$, giving an estimate of three hundred fifteen households. The two estimates differ by forty-five households even though both methods may have been fair.

This difference illustrates sampling variation. It does not automatically prove that one survey was dishonest or that the population changed between surveys. Compare the designs and timing first, then recognize the chance differences expected from observing subsets. Repeated samples and larger well-designed samples can help assess stability, but neither estimate should be presented as an exact census count.

## Handle partial responses honestly

Suppose fifty students are selected, forty respond, and sixteen respondents prefer a new activity. The respondent proportion is $16/40=0.40$. Dividing by fifty would silently treat the ten missing responses as if they did not prefer the activity. Unless that interpretation is explicitly justified, it is incorrect.

However, projecting forty percent to the population also requires caution because the respondents may differ from the nonrespondents. State both the response count and the observed proportion. A complete report might say that sixteen of forty respondents preferred the activity, out of fifty selected students, and that nonresponse may affect the estimate. Arithmetic alone cannot recover the missing preferences.

## Practice projecting counts

A random sample of eighty students contains twenty-four who walk to school. For a school population of five hundred, the estimate is $24/80\cdot500=150$ walkers. Explain why the estimate is one hundred fifty rather than twenty-four: the sample proportion is being extended to a larger population, not merely recounting observed students.

A sample of fifty library users includes seventeen who borrowed an audiobook in the stated month. The proportion is thirty-four percent. For a population of twelve hundred registered users, the projected count is four hundred eight. Reporting about four hundred eight or about four hundred ten can both communicate approximation if the chosen rounding is explained; the exact product is not an exact population measurement.

A survey observes nine successes among thirty sampled cases. The proportion is thirty percent. If the population size doubles while the same estimated proportion is used, the estimated count doubles. The proportion itself does not change just because the population is larger. Separate a relative frequency from the absolute count it predicts.

## Compare estimates responsibly

Two estimates based on different populations or differently worded questions may not be comparable. “Borrowed an audiobook this month” differs from “has ever borrowed an audiobook.” Before interpreting a numerical difference, check the time period, population, definitions, sampling method, and response rate. These details are part of the evidence, not decorations around the calculation.

## Common mistakes

Do not treat missing responses as known negative answers. Do not present a projection as an exact count. Use the sample denominator belonging to the observed subgroup, and multiply by the matching population size. A numerical association from a survey does not by itself identify a cause.

## Key points

- Sample proportion is subgroup count divided by observed sample size.
- Estimated population count is sample proportion times population size.
- Evaluate sampling and response before generalizing.
- Label projections as estimates.
- Differences between fair samples can arise from chance variation.

lessons.title: Compare centers, variability, and overlap
lessons.body:
## Compare distributions, not just single numbers

Two groups can have the same average but very different spreads, or different averages with considerable overlap. A **[[distribution]]** describes how values are arranged and how often they occur. The **[[mean]]** is the sum of numerical values divided by their count. The **[[median]]** is the middle value in an ordered list, or the mean of the two middle values when the count is even. The **[[mean absolute deviation]]** is the mean of the absolute distances of values from their mean.

This lesson uses small, fictional datasets so every calculation can be inspected. Real population comparisons require attention to how samples were selected and measured. A clear numerical difference between two sample means is evidence about those samples; it does not automatically prove a difference for every member of either population.

## Find center before measuring deviation

Consider Group A with values $2,4,4,6$. Their sum is sixteen, so the mean is four. Their ordered middle values are four and four, so the median is also four. The distances from the mean are two, zero, zero, and two. Their average is $(2+0+0+2)/4=1$, so the mean absolute deviation, often abbreviated MAD, is one.

![Dot plots on the same scale show means four and six, equal MADs of one, and overlap between the two fictional groups.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Dot plots on the same scale show means four and six, equal MADs of one, and overlap between the two fictional groups.

The absolute values matter because signed deviations sum to zero around the mean. For Group A, the signed differences are negative two, zero, zero, and positive two. Their sum cancels even though the values are spread out. Taking absolute distances prevents cancellation and measures typical distance from the mean in the original data units.

Now consider Group B with values $4,6,6,8$. Its mean is six and its MAD is one. Group B's center is two units higher, while the two groups have equal variability by this measure. Some values overlap: both groups include four or six. A higher center does not mean every Group B value exceeds every Group A value.

## Compare center difference with variability

The mean difference between the two groups is $6-4=2$. Each group's MAD is one, so the center difference is two MADs. This expresses the separation relative to typical within-group variability. It gives more context than reporting a difference of two without saying how spread out the data are.

Use this comparison most directly when the groups' variability is similar. If one group has MAD one and the other has MAD six, there is no single shared variability value to use casually. Report both spreads and explain the asymmetry rather than selecting whichever denominator makes the difference look more dramatic. At this level, the goal is an informal, evidence-based comparison, not a formal significance test.

### Example 1: Same center, different spread

Group C has values $3,4,4,5$, and Group D has values $0,4,4,8$. Both means are four. For C, distances from four are one, zero, zero, and one, so MAD is $0.5$. For D, distances are four, zero, zero, and four, so MAD is two.

The groups have the same center but different consistency. Group D's values tend to lie farther from the mean. Reporting only the average would hide that difference. A dot plot shows the wider reach of Group D, while the MAD quantifies the typical absolute distance in the same units as the observations.

### Example 2: An extreme value affects the mean

A dataset is $4,5,5,6,20$. The mean is $40/5=8$, while the median is five. The large value twenty pulls the mean above most observations. If the purpose is to describe a typical central observation in this skewed small dataset, the median may be more informative alongside the full display.

Do not delete twenty merely because it is inconvenient. It may be a valid observation, a recording error, or a different kind of case. Investigate its meaning if the study allows, and state any justified exclusion rule. Choosing a center should reflect the question and distribution, not a desire to produce a preferred conclusion.

## Describe overlap in plain language

For Groups A and B, the ranges overlap from four to six. The dot plots show that Group B tends to be higher, but an observation of four could come from either group. A good comparison mentions center, spread, and overlap. Avoid saying “Group B is always greater” when the data themselves contain counterexamples.

If samples were randomly selected from two populations using comparable measures, their distributions may support an informal inference that one population tends to have higher values. The strength of that statement depends on sample size, selection quality, variability, and overlap. A pair of tiny convenient samples gives much weaker population evidence than a well-designed larger comparison.

## Practice calculating and interpreting

For values $1,3,5,7$, the mean is four. Absolute deviations are three, one, one, and three, giving MAD two. The median is also four. Write the deviations before averaging them; skipping that table can make it easy to use squared or signed differences by accident.

For values $5,7,9,11$, the mean is eight and the MAD is also two. Compared with the previous dataset, the mean difference is four, or two MADs. Every value has shifted upward by four, so the spread stays the same. Adding a constant to every observation shifts the center without changing distances from the center.

Two groups have means fifteen and eighteen, with MADs both equal to three. Their mean difference is one MAD. Another pair has the same means but MADs both equal to one. That difference is three MADs. The raw center difference is three in both comparisons, but its size relative to spread differs substantially.

## Make the comparison fair

Use matching units, time periods, and definitions. Comparing reading minutes in one group with reading hours in another requires a unit conversion first. Comparing a five-day total with a seven-day total confounds duration with behavior. A graph should use a common horizontal scale for both groups so differences in spread and location are visually meaningful.

## Common mistakes

Order values before finding the median. Use absolute distances for MAD, not signed differences. Do not infer that a larger mean makes every observation larger. Finally, a difference measured in MAD units is a descriptive comparison here, not a certificate of statistical significance or causation.

## Key points

- Compare center, variability, and overlap together.
- MAD averages absolute distances from the mean.
- Similar variability allows a useful center-difference comparison in MAD units.
- Extreme values can affect the mean strongly.
- Limit population claims to what the sampling design and evidence support.

lessons.title: Investigate variation across samples
lessons.body:
## Different samples can give different answers

A population can stay unchanged while random samples produce different proportions. **[[Sampling variation]]** is the natural difference among statistics from different samples of the same population. **[[Sample size]]** is the number of observations in a sample. **[[Randomization]]** uses a chance process to select outcomes or assignments under a stated rule. A **[[sampling distribution]]** describes how a statistic varies across repeated samples under one sampling method.

The word “variation” does not automatically mean an error or flaw. If one random sample contains twelve supporters out of twenty and another contains nine out of twenty, their proportions differ even when both selections follow the same fair process. Each sample observes a different subset. Recognizing that uncertainty is part of interpreting a sample estimate responsibly.

## Hold the process constant for comparison

To study sampling variation, keep the population, question, sample size, and selection procedure fixed while taking repeated samples. If the population changes between samples or the question is rewritten, differences may have other causes. A controlled simulation can isolate chance variation because its underlying population model is known.

![Illustrative sample percentages distinguish a general stability pattern from an exact prediction.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Illustrative sample percentages distinguish a general stability pattern from an exact prediction.

The figure shows invented illustrative sample percentages from a population model with fifty-percent support. Samples of size twenty yield forty, forty-five, fifty, fifty-five, and sixty percent in the illustration. Samples of size one hundred yield forty-six, forty-eight, fifty, fifty-two, and fifty-four percent. These particular values illustrate a pattern; they are not actual survey results or a guarantee about the next sample.

Under comparable random sampling, larger samples generally produce less variable proportions. More observations tend to balance chance imbalances. This does not mean every larger sample is closer to the population value than every smaller sample. A small sample can happen to be very close, and a larger one can still be unusual. The statement concerns the distribution across repeated samples.

## Build a simple sampling simulation

Use a model bag with equal numbers of two kinds of counters to represent a population with fifty-percent support. To simulate independent selections from this model, draw one counter, record its kind, replace it, and mix before drawing again. Twenty draws form one simulated sample. Count one kind and divide by twenty to obtain the sample proportion.

Repeat many samples, resetting the count after every twenty draws. Plot one point for each sample proportion. Then repeat the entire experiment with one hundred draws per sample. This with-replacement process models independent draws from a fixed probability model. It is not identical to surveying distinct people without replacement from a small finite population; describe which process you are simulating.

### Example 1: Compare two sample estimates

A known model has thirty-percent success probability. One sample of twenty trials has eight successes, giving $8/20=40\%$. Another has five successes, giving twenty-five percent. Both differ from the model's thirty percent, and their estimates differ from each other by fifteen percentage points.

The first sample's estimate is ten percentage points above the model value; the second is five percentage points below it. Neither result alone disproves the model. To evaluate whether the pattern is surprising, examine many repetitions under the same model rather than treating one mismatch as decisive. A theoretical probability is not a promise of an exact count in a short sample.

### Example 2: Compare spread across sample sizes

Suppose a classroom simulation produces sample percentages ranging from thirty-five to sixty-five for size twenty, and from forty-two to fifty-eight for size one hundred. The observed ranges are thirty and sixteen percentage points. In these runs, the larger-sample results are less spread out.

This observation is consistent with the general expectation, but the precise ranges depend on the random runs and the number of repetitions. More repetitions create more opportunities to observe extreme values, so compare experiments with similar numbers of repetitions. Do not treat the smallest and largest observed percentages as permanent limits on what future samples can produce.

## Separate sample size from number of repetitions

A sample of one hundred trials is not the same as one hundred repeated samples of twenty trials each. Sample size controls the amount of information in each estimate. The number of repetitions controls how clearly you can see the distribution of those estimates. Both can be increased, but they answer different questions.

For example, fifty repeated samples of size twenty involve one thousand total draws, yet each plotted sample proportion still comes from only twenty draws. Combining all one thousand draws into one overall proportion creates a different statistic with more information. State whether a plot shows individual observations, separate sample statistics, or one combined total.

## Practice interpreting results

Five simulated samples of ten trials contain four, six, five, three, and seven successes. Their proportions are forty, sixty, fifty, thirty, and seventy percent. The average sample proportion is fifty percent, but individual samples vary widely. Do not replace all five results with fifty when the purpose is to show variation.

Five samples of fifty trials contain twenty-four, twenty-seven, twenty-five, twenty-three, and twenty-six successes. Their proportions are forty-eight, fifty-four, fifty, forty-six, and fifty-two percent. Their mean is also fifty percent, but the observed spread is narrower. Compare these two small illustrations descriptively without claiming they establish an exact uncertainty interval.

A biased survey of one thousand volunteers can still be less representative than a fair random sample of one hundred. Larger size addresses random variability under a suitable design; it does not automatically correct a selection process that systematically favors one response. Keep the earlier sampling-bias lesson separate from the question of chance variation.

## Report uncertainty without overclaiming

A useful summary identifies the model, sample size, number of repetitions, typical estimates, and observed spread. Describe larger-sample results as generally more stable under the same design. Do not invent a formal margin of error from a handful of classroom simulations. Such calculations require methods and assumptions beyond the informal comparisons being made here.

## Common mistakes

A sample proportion need not equal the population proportion. A larger sample is not guaranteed to be closer on every occasion. Sample size differs from repetition count. Finally, the observed simulation range is a description of those runs, not a guaranteed boundary for future outcomes.

## Key points

- Random samples vary even when the population is fixed.
- Compare repeated samples under consistent conditions.
- Larger well-designed samples generally yield more stable proportions.
- Keep sample size and repetition count separate.
- Simulation illustrates uncertainty but does not remove it.

lessons.title: Build probability models
lessons.body:
## Probability describes chance under a model

A spinner, a shuffled set of cards, or a randomly selected counter can have uncertain results. An **[[outcome]]** is one possible result of a chance process. A **[[sample space]]** lists all possible outcomes for that process. An **[[event]]** is a collection of outcomes meeting a condition. **[[Probability]]** is a number from zero to one describing how likely an event is under a stated model.

A probability of zero describes an impossible event in a finite model, while one describes a certain event. Values near zero are unlikely and values near one are likely. One half indicates an event and its complement have equal probabilities. Probability does not state what must happen on one trial; it quantifies uncertainty under assumptions about the process.

## Start with the sample space

For one roll of a fair six-sided number cube, the sample space is $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$. The event “an even number” consists of $\{2,4,6\}$. Because the six individual outcomes are equally likely under the fair-cube model, the probability is the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total: $3/6=1/2$.

![A uniform sample space supports counting favorable outcomes to find event probability.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A uniform sample space supports counting favorable outcomes to find event probability.

The phrase equally likely is essential. Counting outcome labels alone works only when each counted outcome has the same probability. A spinner with one large blue region and one small red region does not necessarily give each color probability one half. The two color names are equally numerous, but their chances depend on the spinner's sector sizes and physical fairness assumptions.

For a spinner divided into equal-area sectors with a fair spin model, count sectors, not merely distinct colors. If four equal sectors are blue and two are red, blue has probability $4/6=2/3$. Multiple basic outcomes can lead to the same named event. A careful sample space records the equally likely units before grouping them by color or other property.

## Models can be nonuniform

A bag contains three red counters, two blue counters, and five green counters. Assume the counters are otherwise identical, mixed well, and equally likely to be drawn. Individual counters are equally likely, but colors are not. The color probabilities are three tenths, two tenths, and five tenths. They add to one because the colors are disjoint and account for every counter.

The event “not green” includes red and blue, with probability $3/10+2/10=5/10$. You can also subtract the green probability from one. An event and its complement partition the whole sample space, so their probabilities sum to one. Be sure the complement is defined relative to the complete sample space, not merely another event that happens to sound different.

### Example 1: A fair number cube

Find the probability of rolling a number greater than four on a fair six-sided cube. The favorable outcomes are five and six, two of the six equally likely outcomes. Thus $P(\text{greater than }4)=2/6=1/3$. The complement, rolling four or less, has probability $4/6=2/3$.

The probabilities add to one, which checks that the two events cover all outcomes without overlap. Rolling exactly four belongs to the complement because the original event is strictly greater than four. If the question said at least four, the favorable set would include four, five, and six, changing the probability to one half.

### Example 2: Unequal color probabilities

A spinner has eight equal sectors: three labeled A, one labeled B, and four labeled C. Under a fair-spin model, $P(A)=3/8$, $P(B)=1/8$, and $P(C)=4/8=1/2$. The event “A or B” has probability four eighths because its sectors do not overlap.

The three labels do not each have probability one third. Their counts of equal sectors differ. Check the model by adding all three probabilities: $3/8+1/8+4/8=1$. If the sectors were unequal in area, sector count alone would no longer establish these probabilities; the model would need the sector sizes or another justified probability assignment.

## Check a proposed probability model

Every probability must be between zero and one, and probabilities of all distinct basic outcomes must sum to one. A list of probabilities $0.2,0.3,0.6$ is invalid for three exhaustive disjoint outcomes because the total is $1.1$. A negative probability is invalid even if other numbers make the sum equal one.

A model can satisfy these numerical rules and still describe a real process poorly. A worn or weighted number cube may not have equally likely faces. The mathematical model states an assumption; experimental evidence can help assess how well that assumption fits. The next lesson compares observed results with theoretical predictions.

## Practice identifying events

For the fair number cube, list the event “a multiple of three”: three and six. Its probability is one third. List “a number less than three”: one and two, also one third. These different events happen to have equal probabilities because they contain the same number of equally likely outcomes.

A bag has four yellow and six purple counters, equally likely individually. The probability of yellow is two fifths, and the probability of purple is three fifths. If one yellow counter is added, the new yellow probability is five elevenths, not one half. Both the favorable count and total count changed, so update the entire fraction.

A probability of $0.75$ means an event is more likely than its complement, which has probability $0.25$. It does not mean the event must happen exactly three times in every four attempts. A four-trial sequence can have fewer or more successes. Probability describes the model across possible outcomes and repeated use, not a short-run quota.

## Common mistakes

Do not assume distinct labels are equally likely. Define the event precisely, especially words such as greater than and at least. Ensure a proposed probability lies between zero and one and that a complete model sums to one. Finally, keep theoretical assumptions separate from observed results.

## Key points

- List basic outcomes and define the event.
- Use favorable count over total only for equally likely outcomes.
- Grouped labels may have unequal probabilities.
- Complement probabilities add to one.
- A valid numerical model still needs justified assumptions about the process.

lessons.title: Compare experiments with probability models
lessons.body:
## Observed frequency and theoretical probability differ

A probability model can predict a chance, while an experiment records what actually happened in a finite run. A **[[trial]]** is one repetition of a chance process. A **[[frequency]]** is the number of times an outcome or event is observed. **[[Relative frequency]]** is event frequency divided by total trials. An **[[experimental probability]]** estimates an event's probability using its observed relative frequency.

Suppose a spinner lands on red eighteen times in sixty trials. The observed relative frequency is $18/60=0.30$. This is the experimental estimate for red in that run. If a geometric spinner model predicts one fourth, the model and observation differ by five percentage points. That difference is evidence to examine, not an automatic proof that the model is false.

## Count consistently and record every trial

Define success before starting. If success is landing on red, record every valid spin as red or not red. Decide in advance how to handle a pointer stopping on a boundary or an interrupted trial. Applying one consistent rule prevents favorable results from being kept while inconvenient results are discarded.

![A cumulative record updates an estimate without double-counting earlier trials.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

A cumulative record updates an estimate without double-counting earlier trials.

A running relative frequency uses all trials completed so far. If the first ten trials contain four successes and the next ten contain three, the twenty-trial frequency is seven and the relative frequency is $7/20=0.35$. It is not the second block's three tenths alone. A table with cumulative trials and cumulative successes helps keep the numerator and denominator aligned.

When combining groups of different sizes, add success counts and trial counts before dividing. One block with two successes in ten and another with eighteen in thirty give twenty successes in forty, or one half. Averaging twenty percent and sixty percent equally would give forty percent, incorrectly treating the unequal blocks as equally large.

## Long-run behavior is not a short-run promise

For repeated independent trials under a stable model, relative frequencies tend to settle closer to the model probability as the number of trials grows. They need not move closer after every new trial. A streak can temporarily move the proportion away again. The tendency concerns long sequences and repeated experiments, not an exact schedule of correction.

If a fair coin has landed heads several times, tails is not “due” on the next independent toss. The next-toss probability remains one half under the fair, independent model. Past outcomes change the observed cumulative frequency but do not change the stated next-trial probability. If the mechanism itself changes, that is a different model requiring new analysis.

### Example 1: Update an experimental estimate

A device produces twelve successes in forty trials. Twenty more trials produce nine additional successes. The new success count is twenty-one, and the new trial count is sixty. Experimental probability is $21/60=0.35$, or thirty-five percent.

The original estimate was $12/40=0.30$, while the second block alone had $9/20=0.45$. The combined result lies between them but is closer to the larger first block's proportion because that block contains twice as many trials. Adding counts automatically gives the correct weighting without needing a separate weighted-average formula.

### Example 2: Predict a count from an estimate

A classroom spinner experiment gives red on thirty-six of one hundred twenty spins, an experimental probability of $0.30$. Using that estimate for two hundred future spins gives an expected count estimate of $0.30(200)=60$ red results. Say “about sixty under this estimate,” not “exactly sixty must occur.”

If the spinner's theoretical model assigns red probability one fourth, that model predicts about fifty red results in two hundred spins. The two predictions use different probability estimates. More carefully controlled observations can help investigate the discrepancy, but a future run remains random under either model. Report which basis you used for the prediction.

## Investigate a discrepancy thoughtfully

A large difference between observed and theoretical results may arise from chance, a poor model, a changing mechanism, or recording mistakes. Check whether the spinner sectors were actually equal, whether the device was used consistently, and whether every valid trial was recorded. Repeating the experiment can provide more evidence, but repeatedly stopping only when results match a preferred answer would distort the process.

At this level, describe the evidence and plausible explanations without inventing a formal certainty threshold. A result of nine heads in ten fair-coin tosses is unusual compared with five in ten, but it remains possible. Saying that any deviation from fifty percent proves unfairness misunderstands the role of probability.

## Practice with cumulative records

A trial table shows five successes after twenty trials, fourteen after forty, and twenty-seven after eighty. The relative frequencies are twenty-five percent, thirty-five percent, and thirty-three point seven five percent. These cumulative counts do not represent three separate blocks to be added; the later row already includes earlier trials.

Two separate experiments contain eight successes in twenty trials and fifteen in thirty trials. Combined, they contain twenty-three in fifty, or forty-six percent. The unweighted average of forty and fifty percent is forty-five percent, which differs because the experiments have different sizes. Explain why trial counts, rather than percentages alone, should be combined.

A fair-model event has probability $0.2$. Over fifty trials, its model-based expected count is ten. A run with eight successes has relative frequency sixteen percent. Both statements can be true: ten is the model's expected count, while eight is what that particular run observed. Neither number should be substituted for the other without explanation.

## Distinguish relative and absolute differences

In a longer run, the success count can be farther from its expected count in absolute units while the relative frequency is closer to the probability. For example, six successes in ten trials differs from five by one but has proportion $0.6$. Five hundred twenty in one thousand differs from five hundred by twenty but has proportion $0.52$, closer to one half. Compare proportions when discussing stabilization.

## Common mistakes

Do not average percentages equally when trial counts differ. Do not add cumulative table rows as if they were separate blocks. A probability is not a quota, and independent events do not become due after a streak. Clearly distinguish observed counts, experimental estimates, and model-based predictions.

## Key points

- Relative frequency is observed successes divided by trials.
- Combine counts before forming a combined proportion.
- Long runs generally stabilize relative frequency under a stable model.
- Each independent next trial retains its modeled probability.
- Predictions describe expected behavior, not guaranteed exact counts.

lessons.title: Organize compound-event sample spaces
lessons.body:
## A compound event combines stages or conditions

Tossing a coin and spinning a numbered spinner creates a result with two parts. A **[[compound event]]** involves more than one condition or stage of a chance process. A **[[tree diagram]]** organizes stages by branching from each earlier outcome to possible later outcomes. **[[Independent events]]** are events for which learning whether one occurred does not change the probability of the other. **[[Replacement]]** means returning a selected object before another draw.

Begin by deciding whether order matters. For two coin tosses, HT and TH are different ordered outcomes: one has heads first, the other tails first. Both belong to the event “exactly one head,” but they are separate equally likely sequences under a fair independent-toss model. Combining them too early can hide their total probability.

## List outcomes systematically

For one fair coin and an independent fair three-sector spinner labeled one, two, and three, the sample space is H1, H2, H3, T1, T2, T3. A table with coin results as rows and spinner results as columns shows all six outcomes without duplication. Each is equally likely because the two devices are fair and the stages are independent.

![An organized two-by-three sample-space table lists each ordered coin-spinner outcome once.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

An organized two-by-three sample-space table lists each ordered coin-spinner outcome once.

The event “heads and an even spinner number” contains only H2, so its probability is one sixth. The event “heads or an even spinner number” contains H1, H2, H3, and T2, so its probability is four sixths, or two thirds. H2 satisfies both conditions but must be counted only once in the “or” event.

A tree provides another organization: branch first into H and T, then from each branch into one, two, and three. Every complete path is one ordered outcome. Count leaves rather than intermediate branch labels. A stage may have a different set of possible next outcomes depending on what happened earlier, especially when objects are not replaced.

## Multiply along paths when the probabilities are known

For independent stages, the probability of one complete path is the product of its stage probabilities. For H2, multiply $\frac12\cdot\frac13=\frac16$. This matches the six-outcome list. For a sequence of events where probabilities change, use the appropriate probability at each stage after accounting for earlier results rather than assuming independence.

The number of possible paths and their probabilities are different issues. A two-stage tree may have four leaves but unequal leaf probabilities. Counting one favorable leaf out of four is valid only if all four leaves are equally likely. Label branch probabilities or reason from equally likely individual objects when the model is nonuniform.

### Example 1: Exactly one head in two tosses

Two independent fair tosses have outcomes HH, HT, TH, and TT, each with probability one fourth. Exactly one head occurs in HT and TH, so its probability is two fourths, or one half. At least one head includes HH as well, so its probability is three fourths.

An incorrect list of “zero heads, one head, two heads” gives three labels but not three equally likely outcomes. One head combines two underlying sequences, while zero and two heads each combine only one. The ordered sample space explains why the middle count has twice the probability of either extreme count.

### Example 2: Draw without replacement

A bag has three red and two blue counters, equally likely individually. Draw one counter, keep it out, then draw a second. Find the probability of red first and blue second. The first probability is three fifths. After a red is removed, four counters remain, including two blue, so the next probability is two fourths. The product is $\frac35\cdot\frac24=\frac3{10}$.

With replacement and mixing, the second blue probability would remain two fifths, giving $\frac35\cdot\frac25=\frac6{25}$. The two answers differ because the process differs. Replacement restores the original composition; without replacement, earlier selections affect later probabilities. Read that condition before calculating.

## Use complements for at least one

For repeated independent trials, “at least one success” can be easier to calculate as one minus “no successes.” With two fair tosses, no heads means TT with probability one fourth, so at least one head has probability three fourths. This complements the direct list HH, HT, TH and provides a check.

For three fair tosses, no heads is TTT with probability one eighth. Therefore at least one head has probability seven eighths. This shortcut avoids listing all seven favorable sequences, but it still depends on a correct complete sample space and the fair independent-toss assumptions. A complement is useful because it partitions the possibilities without overlap.

## Practice with lists and tables

A lunch choice has two sandwich options and three fruit options, with one of each selected. There are six possible combinations by the counting structure. That count does not by itself make all lunches equally likely; people may prefer particular options. If a fair independent random mechanism chooses each category uniformly, then each combination would have probability one sixth. Separate combination counting from probability assumptions.

Two fair independent number cubes have thirty-six ordered outcomes. A sum of two occurs only for $(1,1)$, while a sum of three occurs for $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$. Therefore sums are not all equally likely. The equal-likelihood objects are ordered face pairs, not the eleven possible sum labels from two through twelve.

For the coin-and-three-sector spinner, find “tails or spinner one.” The favorable outcomes are T1, T2, T3, and H1, four out of six. If you add the three tails outcomes and two spinner-one outcomes without adjusting, T1 is counted twice. A marked table makes the overlap visible and helps prevent that error.

## Common mistakes

Do not treat grouped labels as equally likely without checking their underlying outcomes. Distinguish exactly one from at least one. Do not count an overlap twice for an “or” event. Finally, replacement and independence are conditions of the process, not assumptions to insert automatically.

## Key points

- Organize multistage outcomes with a list, table, or tree.
- Keep ordered sequences separate when the process is ordered.
- Multiply stage probabilities using the correct conditions.
- Count overlap once when combining events.
- Complements can simplify at-least-one calculations.

lessons.title: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
topics: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
lessons.body:
## Design a model that can be checked

A **[[simulation]]** uses a simpler chance process to imitate specified features of another process. A **[[model assumption]]** is a condition accepted for the purpose of the model. A **[[success rule]]** defines which complete trial outcomes count toward the event being studied. A **[[validation comparison]]** checks a model or its results against an independent calculation, known benchmark, or relevant evidence.

This capstone combines a fictional school survey, a free activity booth, a prize budget, and a probability simulation. No money is staked by participants. The goal is to connect the course's mathematical tools and explain their limitations. A complete plan should be reproducible: another learner should be able to follow your sampling, calculation, and simulation rules and understand what each result means.

## Define the scenario and the questions

A school has two hundred students. A random sample of fifty students includes thirty who say they plan to visit the booth. The booth has a twenty-dollar fixed supply cost, and each small prize costs one dollar and fifty cents. Its total budget is one hundred dollars. A visitor performs two independent draws with replacement from four equally likely tokens: one star and three circles.

A visitor earns one prize if at least one of the two draws is a star. Two stars still earn only one prize. The questions are: how many visitors should the organizers estimate, what is the modeled chance of a prize per visitor, how many prizes can the budget buy, and does the expected prize count guarantee enough supply? Keep these as separate quantities before combining them.

![The capstone keeps participation, individual success probability, supply limits, and whole-event risk as distinct quantities.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The capstone keeps participation, individual success probability, supply limits, and whole-event risk as distinct quantities.

The survey estimates participation, while the token model describes prizes conditional on a visit. They are different evidence sources. The survey does not prove that exactly the estimated number will attend. The fair-token model also does not guarantee an exact number of prize-winning visits. Combining estimates does not remove their uncertainty.

### Example 1: Participation and budget

The sample participation proportion is $30/50=0.60$. Applying it to two hundred students gives an estimate of one hundred twenty visitors. Label this as a projection based on the sample and stated intentions, which can differ from actual attendance. A well-selected sample improves the inference but cannot force future behavior to match it.

For prizes, let $p$ be the nonnegative whole-number count purchased. The budget condition is $20+1.5p\le100$. Subtract twenty and divide by $1.5$ to get $p\le53\frac13$. The maximum whole count is fifty-three. Check: fifty-three prizes cost $79.50$, plus twenty gives $99.50$; fifty-four prizes would make the total $101$, exceeding the budget.

### Example 2: Probability and expected demand

For one draw, the chance of no star is three fourths. Replacement and mixing restore that chance before the second draw. The chance of no star on either draw is $\frac34\cdot\frac34=\frac9{16}$. Therefore the chance of at least one star is $1-\frac9{16}=\frac7{16}$.

For an assumed one hundred twenty visitors, the modeled expected prize count is $120\cdot\frac7{16}=52.5$. An expected count can be fractional even though an actual count must be whole. It represents the model's average demand across repetitions, not half of a physical prize. Fifty-three prizes are only slightly above this expectation and do not guarantee enough for every possible outcome; up to all visitors could qualify under the model.

## Specify a faithful random mechanism

A fair random integer from one through four can represent each token draw. Assign one to star and two, three, and four to circle. Generate two independent integers for one visitor, and count success if either integer is one. Reset for the next visitor. This mapping gives the star exactly one fourth probability per draw and preserves the replacement assumption.

A fair coin with heads for star would be wrong because it gives one half instead of one fourth. Drawing two tokens without replacement would also be wrong because the second-draw probabilities change. The simulation must match the structure of the model, not just produce a sequence of random-looking symbols.

## Record complete visitor trials

Make a table with visitor-trial number, first draw, second draw, and prize yes or no. The pair $(1,1)$ counts as one successful visitor, not two prizes. For an initial practice run, generate thirty-two visitor trials, or sixty-four individual draws. Calculate successful visitors divided by thirty-two and compare it with seven sixteenths.

For illustration, suppose twelve of thirty-two visitor trials succeed. The observed proportion is $12/32=0.375$, while the theoretical probability is $0.4375$. The difference is $0.0625$, or six point two five percentage points. These are invented demonstration results, not evidence that an experiment was actually performed. A real run should preserve its actual records, even when they differ from the theory.
