questions.stem: Why can two fair random samples have different proportions?
choices: They observe different subsets by chance.
questions.explanation: Chance variation occurs even with a fixed population.

questions.stem: Under comparable fair sampling, what generally happens as sample size grows?
questions.explanation: More observations generally stabilize a sample proportion, without guaranteeing perfection.

questions.stem: What is the sample size in 30 repeated samples of 20 observations each?
questions.explanation: Each estimate is based on twenty observations.

questions.stem: A sample has 7 successes in 20 trials. What is its proportion?
questions.explanation: Seven divided by twenty is 0.35.

questions.stem: What does the range of observed simulated estimates describe?
choices: Every possible future sample with certainty
A guaranteed formal margin of error
questions.explanation: Future samples can fall outside an observed finite-run range.

questions.stem: Why replace and remix a counter in an independent-draw model?
choices: To restore the same probabilities for the next draw
questions.explanation: Replacement keeps the modeled composition fixed.

questions.stem: Can a larger biased sample remain biased?
choices: Only if the population is zero
questions.explanation: Systematic selection problems are not cured by count alone.

questions.stem: What must stay fixed to isolate sampling variation?
questions.explanation: Repeated runs vary by chance while their underlying process stays consistent.

questions.stem: Select all correct interpretations.
choices: A small sample may happen to be very accurate.
Every larger sample beats every smaller sample.
A larger sample is generally more stable across repetitions.
Observed minimum and maximum are guaranteed future bounds.
questions.explanation: General stability is a repeated-sampling pattern, not an absolute promise for each run.

questions.stem: Give only the percent number: 18 successes in 40 trials produce ___%.
questions.explanation: Eighteen divided by forty is 0.45.

questions.stem: Give only the total draws: 25 samples of 20 draws each use ___ draws.
questions.explanation: Multiply the number of repetitions by sample size.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: Natural differences among statistics from samples of the same population.
The number of observations in a sample.
Use of a chance process under a stated selection or assignment rule.
The distribution of a statistic across repeated samples under one method.
questions.explanation: Read the quantities and conditions as well as the vocabulary. sampling variation: Natural differences among statistics from samples of the same population. sample size: The number of observations in a sample. randomization: Use of a chance process under a stated selection or assignment rule. sampling distribution: The distribution of a statistic across repeated samples under one method.

questions.stem: What is the probability of an even number on a fair six-sided number cube?
questions.explanation: Three of six equally likely faces are even.

questions.stem: Which number cannot be a probability?
questions.explanation: Probabilities cannot exceed one.

questions.stem: A bag has 3 red and 7 blue equally likely counters. What is P(red)?
questions.explanation: Three of the ten individual counters are red.

questions.stem: If P(A)=0.35, what is P(not A)?
questions.explanation: Complement probabilities sum to one.

questions.stem: A spinner has 6 equal sectors: 4 A and 2 B. What is P(A)?
questions.explanation: Count equal sectors, not just distinct labels.

questions.stem: Which event on a fair number cube has probability 1/3?
questions.explanation: A number greater than four means five or six: two of six equally likely faces. At least four, odd, and less than six have different favorable counts.

questions.stem: What must probabilities of all disjoint exhaustive outcomes sum to?
questions.explanation: The full sample space has probability one.

questions.stem: When is favorable count divided by total count directly justified?
choices: Only when the result is one half
For any unequal outcomes without adjustment
When the counted outcomes are equally likely
questions.explanation: Equal-likelihood units are required for the counting ratio.

questions.stem: Select all valid probability values.
questions.explanation: Valid probabilities lie in the closed interval from zero to one.

questions.stem: Give an exact fraction: on a fair six-sided cube, P(rolling 1)=___.
questions.explanation: One of six equally likely outcomes is favorable.

questions.stem: Give only the decimal: if P(A)=0.7, P(not A)=___.
questions.explanation: Subtract 0.7 from one.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: One possible result of a chance process.
The complete collection of possible outcomes for a chance process.
A collection of outcomes satisfying a stated condition.
A number from zero to one describing an event’s chance under a model.
questions.explanation: Read the quantities and conditions as well as the vocabulary. outcome: One possible result of a chance process. sample space: The complete collection of possible outcomes for a chance process. event: A collection of outcomes satisfying a stated condition. probability: A number from zero to one describing an event’s chance under a model.

questions.stem: An event occurs 9 times in 30 trials. What is experimental probability?
questions.explanation: Divide frequency by trial count.

questions.stem: Two separate runs have 4 successes in 10 and 18 in 30. What is combined relative frequency?
questions.explanation: Add both success counts and both trial counts; the result is 0.55.

questions.stem: After five heads on independent fair-coin tosses, what is P(tails next)?
questions.explanation: Independence keeps the next-toss probability unchanged.

questions.stem: A probability estimate is 0.4. What count is predicted for 150 trials?
questions.explanation: Multiply 0.4 by 150, while retaining random variation.

questions.stem: What does a cumulative frequency row include?
choices: Only the most recent trial automatically
questions.explanation: Cumulative counts include preceding observations.

questions.stem: Must relative frequency move closer to the model after every trial?
choices: Yes, if the event is possible
questions.explanation: Random fluctuations can move it temporarily farther away.

questions.stem: Why not equally average percentages from unequal run sizes?
choices: Every combined probability is one half.
The runs contribute different numbers of observations.
questions.explanation: Combine counts to weight each observation equally.

questions.stem: A model predicts 25% success, but a run gives 30%. What can be said immediately?
choices: The observed estimate differs from the model.
questions.explanation: A discrepancy can occur by chance or from model and procedure issues; it needs investigation.

questions.stem: Select all sound experimental practices.
choices: Discard outcomes that disagree with the model.
Record every valid trial under one stated rule.
Stop only when the desired percentage appears.
questions.explanation: Consistent definitions and complete recording avoid selecting favorable evidence.

questions.stem: Give only the percent number: 16 successes in 80 trials represent ___%.
questions.explanation: Sixteen divided by eighty is one fifth.

questions.stem: Give only the predicted count: an estimate of 0.35 over 200 trials predicts about ___ successes.
questions.explanation: Multiply 0.35 by two hundred.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: One repetition of a chance process.
The number of times an outcome or event is observed.
Event frequency divided by the total number of trials.
A probability estimate based on observed relative frequency.
questions.explanation: Read the quantities and conditions as well as the vocabulary. trial: One repetition of a chance process. frequency: The number of times an outcome or event is observed. relative frequency: Event frequency divided by the total number of trials. experimental probability: A probability estimate based on observed relative frequency.

questions.stem: How many ordered outcomes occur in two fair coin tosses?
questions.explanation: They are HH, HT, TH, and TT.

questions.stem: What is P(exactly one head) in two independent fair tosses?
questions.explanation: HT and TH are two of four equally likely outcomes.

questions.stem: What is P(at least one head) in two independent fair tosses?
questions.explanation: Only TT is excluded.

questions.stem: A fair coin and independent fair four-sector spinner have how many equally likely ordered outcomes?
questions.explanation: Two coin outcomes times four spinner outcomes gives eight.

questions.stem: Why are sums of two fair number cubes not equally likely?
choices: The cubes have no sample space.
Different sums contain different numbers of ordered face pairs.
Order never matters in the underlying outcomes.
questions.explanation: Count the thirty-six equally likely ordered pairs before grouping by sum.

questions.stem: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue. After a red draw without replacement, what is P(blue next)?
questions.explanation: Four counters remain, including both blue counters.

questions.stem: What does replacement restore in a well-mixed counter model?
questions.explanation: Returning the counter restores the counts before the next draw.

questions.stem: When counting A or B, what happens to outcomes in both?
questions.explanation: An outcome is one member of the union even if it meets both conditions.

questions.stem: Select all sequences with exactly two heads in three tosses.
questions.explanation: HHT and HTH each contain exactly two heads. THH would also qualify but is not listed; HHH has three heads and TTT has none.

questions.stem: Give an exact fraction: P(no heads in three independent fair tosses)=___.
questions.explanation: Only TTT among eight equally likely sequences has no heads.

questions.stem: Give only the count: 3 shirt choices and 4 hat choices make ___ distinct shirt-hat combinations.
questions.explanation: Each of three shirts pairs with four hats.

questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: An event involving multiple conditions or stages of a chance process.
A branching representation of sequential outcomes.
Events for which learning one occurred does not change the probability of the other.
Returning a selected object before the next draw.
questions.explanation: Read the quantities and conditions as well as the vocabulary. compound event: An event involving multiple conditions or stages of a chance process. tree diagram: A branching representation of sequential outcomes. independent events: Events for which learning one occurred does not change the probability of the other. replacement: Returning a selected object before the next draw.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: A token model has one star among four equally likely tokens. Which integer mapping matches it?
choices: Star on 1 or 2; circle on 3 or 4
Star only after a previous circle
questions.explanation: One of four equally likely integer outcomes must represent star.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: For two independent replacement draws, what is P(at least one star) if P(star)=1/4?
questions.explanation: Subtract the no-star probability nine sixteenths from one.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: What is one trial when studying whether a visitor wins a prize?
choices: Every visitor in the school year
questions.explanation: The success rule concerns the complete two-draw visit.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: A visitor draws two stars but earns at most one prize. How many prizes count?
questions.explanation: The stated rule awards one prize for at least one star.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: What does expected demand 52.5 mean?
choices: Exactly 52.5 physical prizes in one event
Proof that supplies cannot run out
questions.explanation: Expected counts can be fractional while actual counts remain whole and variable.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: Which simulation estimates the chance of a whole-event shortage?
choices: Repeat full events and count those whose demand exceeds supply.
Divide star draws by all draws.
Stop whenever supply is exactly used.
questions.explanation: The trial unit must be a whole event when the event of interest is shortage.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: Why label demonstration data as invented?
choices: To distinguish illustrations from collected evidence
questions.explanation: Honest reporting separates example records from actual observations.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: What should a reproducible simulation specify?
choices: Mapping, trial unit, success rule, and repetition procedure
questions.explanation: These details let another person repeat the modeled process.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: Select all limitations of the booth model.
choices: Expected demand is a guaranteed exact count.
A budget maximum automatically guarantees enough prizes.
Actual attendance may differ from the survey estimate.
Token draws may fail the independence assumption if the procedure changes.
questions.explanation: Attendance and process assumptions can fail; expectation and budget limits do not guarantee supply.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: Give only the estimated visitor count: 24 of 40 sampled students plan to attend, from a population of 300. Estimate ___ visitors.
questions.explanation: The sample proportion 0.6 times three hundred gives one hundred eighty.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: Give only the maximum whole prize count: a 10-dollar fixed cost and 2 dollars per prize must fit 75 dollars, so at most ___ prizes fit.
questions.explanation: The bound is 32.5 prizes, and thirty-two is the feasible whole maximum.

questions.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
questions.stem: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.
choices: A simpler chance process used to imitate specified features of another process.
A condition accepted for the purpose of a model.
A definition of which complete trial outcomes count as the event of interest.
A check against an independent calculation, known benchmark, or relevant evidence.
questions.explanation: Read the quantities and conditions as well as the vocabulary. simulation: A simpler chance process used to imitate specified features of another process. model assumption: A condition accepted for the purpose of a model. success rule: A definition of which complete trial outcomes count as the event of interest. validation comparison: A check against an independent calculation, known benchmark, or relevant evidence.

cards.back: A number whose sign indicates direction relative to zero.
A number expressible as a fraction of integers with a nonzero denominator.
A line on which equal distances represent equal numerical differences.
A number that adds to a given number to make zero.

cards.front: How can you check the sign of a mixed-sign sum?
cards.back: Cancel equal opposite amounts. The sign of the uncanceled amount is the sign of the sum.
The result of subtracting one number from another.
The final value minus the initial value, including its sign.
A nonnegative measure of separation.
The distance of a number from zero.

cards.front: How do directed change and distance differ?
cards.back: Directed change is final minus initial and can be negative. Distance is the absolute value of the difference.
A quantity being multiplied.
The result of multiplication.
The rule a(b+c)=ab+ac, connecting multiplication and addition.
The result of division by a nonzero divisor.

cards.front: Why is division by zero undefined?
cards.back: A nonzero dividend cannot equal zero times a quotient; for zero divided by zero, no unique quotient is determined.
A decimal with finitely many nonzero decimal places.
cards.topic: Fractions, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals

cards.back: A decimal with a digit block that repeats forever from some point onward.
cards.topic: Fractions, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals

cards.back: The amount left after removing whole copies of a divisor in a division step.
cards.topic: Fractions, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals

cards.back: The difference introduced by replacing an exact value with a rounded value.
cards.topic: Fractions, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals

cards.front: How can you predict whether a fraction terminates?
cards.back: Reduce it first. Its positive denominator must have only prime factors two and five.
cards.topic: Fractions, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals

cards.back: A comparison of quantities measured in different units.
A rate expressed for one unit of the denominator quantity.
A number that multiplies a given nonzero number to make one.
A check that the units of a calculation match the requested quantity.

cards.front: How do you decide the order of division for a rate?
cards.back: Write the requested units. The quantity after “per” is the divisor.
A relationship expressible as y=kx for a fixed constant k.
The fixed ratio of output to nonzero input in a proportional relationship.
A quantity supplied to a rule.
The quantity a rule determines from its input.

cards.front: What disproves a proportional model for a table?
cards.back: One nonzero-input ratio differing from the others, or a pair with zero input and nonzero output.
Two coordinates written in the order input first, output second.
The point (0,0) where the coordinate axes meet.
The point (1,k) on the graph of y=kx.
The numerical amount represented by each equal spacing on an axis.

cards.front: What two graph features identify proportionality?
cards.back: A straight line through the origin, with the displayed points restricted to inputs allowed by the context.
A representation using one fixed multiplicative relationship for corresponding lengths.
A statement connecting a length on a drawing with an actual length.
A multiplier between corresponding lengths expressed in matching units.
A length matching the same feature in another figure.

cards.front: How does a length scale factor affect area?
cards.back: Multiply area by the square of the length factor, because both length dimensions change.
The change divided by the original positive amount, expressed as a percent.
The starting quantity used as the reference for a change.
The quantity after a change has occurred.
The absolute discrepancy divided by a positive accepted reference value, expressed as a percent.

cards.front: Which reference belongs in percent error?
cards.back: The stated accepted value, using the absolute discrepancy in the numerator.
An increase calculated from a stated cost or other stated base.
A reduction from a stated price.
An added charge based on a taxable amount under a stated rule.
A factor that directly converts a base amount into a resulting amount.

cards.front: Why can you not usually subtract a discount rate from a tax rate?
cards.back: The rates may apply to different bases. Use the specified sequence of multipliers.
Interest calculated on the original principal for the stated time.
The original amount used as the base for an interest calculation.
An additional payment calculated here from a specified bill amount.
A payment calculated as a percent of a stated sales amount or other specified base.

cards.front: What units must agree in the interest formula?
cards.back: The rate period and the time unit must match; an annual rate requires time in years.
A problem asking for a base from a known percent relationship and resulting amount.
cards.topic: Find an original amount and compare percent changes

cards.back: The share of an original amount left after a decrease.
cards.topic: Find an original amount and compare percent changes

cards.back: The product of the multipliers for successive changes.
cards.topic: Find an original amount and compare percent changes

cards.back: The overall relative change from the initial amount to the final amount.
cards.topic: Find an original amount and compare percent changes

cards.front: How do you find a net percent change from multiplier m?
cards.back: For a positive original amount, calculate (m−1)×100%; a negative result indicates a decrease.
cards.topic: Find an original amount and compare percent changes

cards.back: A combination of numbers, variables, and operations representing a quantity.
A part of a sum, including its sign.
The numerical factor multiplying a variable part.
Terms with identical variable parts and exponents.

cards.front: Why does x+x equal 2x rather than x squared?
cards.back: It adds two copies of x. Squaring would multiply x by x.
Rewrite a product involving a sum or difference as separate terms.
Rewrite a sum or difference as a product.
A factor shared by every term being factored.
An expression with variables only to the first power and no products of variables.

cards.front: What is the safest check after factoring?
cards.back: Distribute the factor back across every term and confirm that the original expression returns.
Expressions with the same value for every allowed value of their variables.
The amount to which a rate or change is applied.
An amount that stays unchanged as the variable quantity changes.
An amount that changes according to the value of a variable.

cards.front: How do you choose among equivalent forms?
cards.back: Use the form that exposes the quantity or relationship the question asks about, while preserving the stated base and grouping.
An approximate value used for planning or checking.
A familiar reference value used to judge or simplify a calculation.
A condition that an acceptable result must satisfy.
How finely a value is stated or measured.

cards.front: When should you round up a package count?
cards.back: When only whole packages are available and the requirement is a minimum that must be met.
A statement that two expressions have equal values.
A value that makes a stated equation or inequality true.
An operation that undoes another operation.
Applying the same valid operation to both sides preserves an equation.
It verifies that the proposed value satisfies the relationship before any potentially mistaken transformation.
An expression treated as one unit by an operation.
An equation with the same solution set as another over the stated domain.
Rewrite an equation with the variable alone on one side.
Substitution of a proposed value into the original statement.

cards.front: What two methods solve a grouped linear equation?
cards.back: Divide by the nonzero outside factor first, or distribute first and solve the resulting equation.
A comparison using less than, greater than, or a version allowing equality.
All allowed values that make a mathematical statement true.
A value where the compared expressions would be equal.
An open or closed graph marker indicating whether a boundary is included.

cards.front: Why reverse order after multiplying by a negative?
cards.back: Negative scaling reflects positions across zero, reversing which values lie to the left and right.
A value satisfying every stated condition and domain restriction.
The least allowed or required value in a stated setting.
The greatest allowed value in a stated setting.
A limit on which values a variable may represent.

cards.front: How do you interpret a fractional boundary for an item count?
cards.back: Choose the nearest whole count that actually satisfies the limit, then test the neighboring excluded count.
Angles whose measures sum to ninety degrees.
Angles whose measures sum to one hundred eighty degrees.
Opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines; their measures are equal.
Adjacent angles whose nonshared sides form a straight line.

cards.front: How can you justify equal vertical angles?
cards.back: Each is supplementary to the same adjacent angle, so subtracting that shared angle from 180 gives equal measures.
The requirement that any two triangle side lengths sum to more than the third.
A triangle determined in size and shape, allowing movement, rotation, or reflection.
Triangles with equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.
The angle between two specified sides.

cards.front: Why do three angles allow many triangles?
cards.back: They fix shape but not scale; enlarged and reduced similar copies retain the same angles.
A segment from the center of a circle to its boundary, or its length.
A segment across a circle through its center, with length twice the radius.
The distance around a circle.
The exact constant ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

cards.front: Why is area proportional to radius squared?

references.title: Math 7 study guide, readiness check, and capstone rubric
references.body:
## How to study this course

Work through the nine modules in order. Math 6 supplies the prerequisite fraction, ratio, expression, and data foundations. Each lesson has original teaching, two worked examples, a diagram, practice explanations, twelve questions, and two generated drills. Module checkpoints select questions from the lesson bank; they are not additional unseen bank questions.

Read a worked example with its answer covered, attempt the next step, then compare the reason as well as the result. Use the figure's caption to connect its labels to the calculation. Diagrams are illustrative unless a task explicitly requests measurement. Keep a notebook for diagrams, algebra steps, sample-space lists, and explanations that the automatic answer checker cannot fully evaluate.

For a missed question, identify whether the difficulty was interpretation, arithmetic, notation, or a model assumption. Review the matching reference and attempt another generated drill. A correct final number is useful evidence, but explaining the method and checking the original conditions shows more understanding than repeatedly guessing among choices.

## Readiness check

Try these tasks before Module 1. These are an ungraded diagnostic, not an additional automated quiz. Use the explanations below to choose a review topic.

1. Compute $\frac34+\frac16$.
2. Compute $\frac56\div\frac23$.
3. Write $0.35$ as a percent.
4. Find the price per kilogram for six dollars and two and a half kilograms.
5. Evaluate $3x+4$ when $x=5$.
6. Find the area of a triangle with base eight and perpendicular height three.
7. Find the volume of a two-by-three-by-four rectangular prism.
8. Find the mean and median of $2,4,5,9$.
9. Find the distance between $-3$ and $2$ on a number line.
10. Simplify the ratio twelve to eighteen.

## Readiness explanations

1. Use twelfths: nine twelfths plus two twelfths gives eleven twelfths. Review fraction addition if the denominators were added.
2. Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor: $\frac56\cdot\frac32=\frac54$. Review fraction division if both fractions were inverted.
3. Thirty-five hundredths is thirty-five percent. Check the direction of the hundred-fold conversion.
4. Divide six dollars by $2.5$ kilograms to obtain $2.40$ per kilogram. Keep cost in the numerator for this requested rate.
5. Substitute five for the entire variable: three times five plus four gives nineteen.
6. Half of eight times three is twelve square units. The height must be perpendicular to the chosen base.
7. Multiply the three perpendicular dimensions to obtain twenty-four cubic units.
8. The sum is twenty, so the mean is five. The two middle ordered values are four and five, giving median $4.5$.
9. The separation is five units: three to zero and two more to the positive endpoint.
10. Divide both quantities by six to obtain two to three. Preserve the requested order.

## Module evidence checklist

| Module | Explain without looking at a formula sheet |
|---|---|
| Rational numbers | Why subtraction adds an inverse and why negative times negative is positive |
| Proportional relationships | How units, a constant ratio, an equation, and a graph describe one model |
| Percent applications | Which amount is the base and how to reverse the resulting multiplier |
| Expressions | Why two forms are equivalent and which form best reveals the requested quantity |
| Equations and inequalities | Why each transformation preserves a solution set, including negative scaling |
| Plane geometry | Which stated relationship justifies each angle, area, or perimeter equation |
| Solids | Which dimensions or faces belong to a section, volume, or surface-area calculation |
| Statistics | What the sample supports and what uncertainty or bias remains |
| Probability | Which outcomes are equally likely and what one complete simulation trial means |

## Capstone evidence and feedback

The final lesson provides a fictional free activity-booth scenario. Prepare a report rather than only a final number. Use this ten-point self-review or instructor review rubric; it is not a claim of an automatically scored project.

| Criterion | Points | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|
| Population and sample | 2 | Correct population, sample proportion, projected count, and estimate language |
| Budget and domain | 2 | Correct inequality, whole-number maximum, and check of the excluded neighbor |
| Probability model | 2 | Correct two-draw sample structure, replacement assumptions, and at-least-one probability |
| Simulation design | 2 | Correct mapping, trial unit, success rule, records, and repetition plan |
| Interpretation | 2 | Distinguishes expectation from guarantee and identifies a meaningful limitation |

For each criterion, award two when the calculation and explanation are correct, one when the main idea is present but a specific correction is needed, and zero when the evidence is missing or represents a different quantity. Write the correction in words. A proposed simulation can earn design credit without falsely claiming that it was run; actual result claims require actual recorded trials.

## Answer and notation habits

Use exact fractions when requested, and follow explicit rounding instructions for decimals. A text-answer prompt asking only for a number should receive that number without extra units; keep the interpretation in your notebook. A select-all question can have several correct choices. Matching questions assess vocabulary and relationships, while drills generate new numerical instances.

Keep estimates, exact calculations, observed data, and assumptions distinguishable. Use an approximately-equal sign or words such as about for rounded or projected quantities. If a real task lacks a necessary condition, state the missing information rather than inventing a precise answer. This habit is especially important in sampling, probability, geometric diagrams, and practical constraints.

references.title: Rational numbers — quick reference
references.body:
## Signed-number decisions

Choose what zero and each direction mean. Addition combines changes; subtraction finds a difference. Rewrite $a-b$ as $a+(-b)$. A directed change is final minus initial, while distance is $|a-b|$ and cannot be negative.

| Operation | Decision | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Same-sign addition | Add magnitudes; keep the sign. | Two drops should not create a rise. |
| Opposite-sign addition | Cancel equal opposite amounts. | Use the sign of what remains. |
| Subtraction | Add the inverse of the subtracted number. | Add the change back to the initial value. |
| Product or quotient | Equal nonzero signs give positive; different signs give negative. | Check magnitude separately. |

Division by zero is undefined. Zero divided by a nonzero number is zero. Parentheses matter: $(-3)^2=9$, while $-3^2=-9$.

## Fraction and decimal representations

Use common denominators for addition and subtraction. For fraction division, multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor. Long division terminates when a remainder reaches zero; a repeated nonzero remainder creates repeating digits. Reduce a fraction before testing whether its denominator has only prime factors two and five.

Exact and rounded answers differ: $\frac13=0.\overline3$, but $\frac13\approx0.33$. Retain exact values until the requested rounding stage. A useful final check asks whether the sign, size, units, and precision all match the question.

references.title: Proportional relationships — quick reference
references.body:
## Proportional reasoning

Write the requested units before dividing. Kilometers per hour means distance divided by time; hours per kilometer reverses that order. Fractional quantities follow the same rule: $\frac34\div\frac12=\frac32$.

A proportional relationship is $y=kx$. For nonzero inputs, every $y/x$ must equal the same constant. The pair $(0,0)$ is necessary but does not prove proportionality by itself. A fixed fee usually produces a rule such as $y=kx+b$ with nonzero $b$, which is not proportional.

A continuous proportional graph is straight and passes through the origin. The point $(1,k)$ displays the unit rate. An ordered pair must be interpreted using the axis definitions, and axis scales can change a line's apparent steepness. Whole-object contexts may permit only selected points on the line.

## Scale drawings

Match corresponding lengths and label conversion direction. At one centimeter to four meters, a three-centimeter drawing segment represents twelve meters. For a dimensionless ratio, convert to matching units: one centimeter to four meters is $1:400$.

A uniform length factor $s$ multiplies perimeter by $s$ and area by $s^2$. Redrawing at a different scale changes the representation, not the actual object. A resized image may invalidate a printed numeric scale unless the intended print size or a matching scale bar is used.

references.title: Percent applications — quick reference
references.body:
## Choose the percent base

Convert a percent to a decimal by dividing by one hundred. Identify the base before calculating any part or total.

| Task | Relationship for a positive base |
|---|---|
| Percent change | $(\text{new}-\text{original})/\text{original}\cdot100\%$ |
| Percent error | $|\text{estimate}-\text{accepted}|/\text{accepted}\cdot100\%$ |
| Increase at decimal rate $r$ | New amount $=(1+r)\times$ original |
| Decrease at decimal rate $r$ | New amount $=(1-r)\times$ original |
| Reverse a change | Original $=$ new amount divided by its nonzero multiplier |
| Simple interest | $I=Prt$; total amount $A=P+I$ |

Annual simple-interest rates require time in years. A nine-month interval is three fourths year. Simple interest keeps the original principal as its base; it does not compound.

Successive percentages use successive bases. A twenty-percent increase followed by a twenty-percent decrease has multiplier $1.2(0.8)=0.96$, a four-percent net decrease. Equal rates do not generally cancel.

Tax, tip, markup, and commission exercises use the explicitly stated fictional rules. Include fixed fees separately and round at the specified stage. A zero original or accepted amount makes the usual relative-percent formulas undefined. Percentage-point change subtracts two percentages; relative percent change divides by the original percentage.

references.title: Expressions and numerical reasoning — quick reference
references.body:
## Expressions preserve quantities

A term includes its sign. Combine terms only when their variable parts and exponents match. Add the coefficients while leaving that variable part unchanged: $\frac12x+\frac14x=\frac34x$. Constants combine with constants. Unlike terms such as $a$ and $b$ remain separate unless another relationship is supplied.

Distribution expands a product: $a(b+c)=ab+ac$. A negative factor affects every term, so $-2(x-3)=-2x+6$. Factoring reverses distribution: $6x+9=3(2x+3)$. Re-expand a proposed factorization to check every term.

Equivalent forms can reveal different features. In $4(t+3)$, parentheses show one complete package; $4t+12$ separates all variable costs from all fixed package charges. A fixed charge added once differs from a charge included in every package.

## Multistep problem routine

1. Name the target quantity and units.
2. Write a relationship or grouped expression matching the story.
3. Keep exact values until rounding is required.
4. Use an estimate or benchmark to check size and decimal placement.
5. Apply practical constraints and explain the final answer.

A requirement for at least twenty-five items in packs of six needs five packs, even though ordinary nearest-integer rounding of $25/6$ gives four. A complete-groups question uses a different interpretation. Arithmetic and context must both support the result.

references.title: Equations and inequalities — quick reference
references.body:
## Preserve the relationship

For an equation, apply the same valid operation to both sides. To solve $3x+5=26$, subtract five and divide by three, giving seven. For $3(x+4)=30$, divide by three and subtract four, giving six; expanding first is also valid.

Always substitute into the original equation. The intermediate value of a group may differ from the unknown part requested. Equality does not reverse when dividing by a negative number.

## Inequality decisions

| Transformation or notation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Add or subtract the same amount | Keep comparison direction. |
| Multiply or divide by a positive amount | Keep comparison direction. |
| Multiply or divide by a negative amount | Reverse comparison direction. |
| Strict inequality, $<$ or $>$ | Use an open endpoint. |
| Equality allowed, $\le$ or $\ge$ | Use a closed endpoint. |

For $-2x+3\le11$, the solution is $x\ge-4$. Test the boundary and one value on each side. The endpoint and shaded direction are separate decisions.

Combine algebraic bounds with domain restrictions. A nonnegative whole-number count satisfying $n\le6.75$ has maximum six. A minimum requirement $p\ge4.2$ needs at least five whole packages. Two constraints can conflict, leaving no feasible value. Do not round an equation's solution and claim it still satisfies the exact equation.

references.title: Plane geometry — quick reference
references.body:
## Angles and triangles

Complementary measures sum to ninety degrees; supplementary measures sum to one hundred eighty. Vertical angles are equal. A linear pair is adjacent with nonshared sides forming a straight line. Angles around a point total three hundred sixty. Write an equation from the relationship, then substitute the solved variable into the requested angle expression.

Triangle angles total one hundred eighty degrees and must each be positive. The sum of any two sides must strictly exceed the third. Equality makes a flat arrangement. Three valid side lengths determine one size and shape, allowing movement and reflection. Two sides with the included angle also determine one triangle. Three angles alone leave size undetermined.

## Circles and composite regions

Diameter is $2r$. Circumference is $C=\pi d=2\pi r$ in length units. Area is $A=\pi r^2$ in square units. Use the supplied approximation of pi only when approximating; an exact pi expression remains exact.

A semicircle's full perimeter includes its diameter in addition to the curved half-circumference. For composite regions, add nonoverlapping areas or subtract a cutout from a surrounding region. For perimeter, trace the requested boundary and exclude internal dividing lines. Two regions joined along an edge require removing that shared edge twice from their added perimeters.

Use stated dimensions rather than measuring a schematic illustration. Distinguish the variable value, angle measure, area, and perimeter in the final answer.

references.title: Solids and measurement — quick reference
references.body:
## Solids and their slices

A cross-section is a plane's intersection with a solid. Position and orientation determine the section. An interior slice of a rectangular prism parallel to a face is a congruent rectangle. A corner cut can instead be triangular. Base-parallel sections of a pyramid shrink toward its apex; a plane through the apex and an appropriate base segment can make a triangle.

## Volume and surface area

For a right prism, $V=Bh$, with complete base area $B$ and perpendicular prism height $h$. A triangular base uses $B=\frac12ba$, where $a$ is its own perpendicular altitude. Do not confuse that triangle altitude with the prism length.

A closed right prism's surface area is $2B+Ph$, where $P$ is base perimeter. For a rectangular prism, this is $2(lw+lh+wh)$. A net helps inventory faces. Omit an absent top only when the task says it is open. Pyramid side-triangle areas use slant heights within those faces, not an unrelated vertical height.

Add volumes of solids with nonoverlapping interiors. Subtract cavity volume to find remaining material. For exposed surface area of joined pieces, subtract twice each shared contact face from summed individual surface areas.

Uniform length factor $s$ gives area factor $s^2$ and volume factor $s^3$. Changing only one dimension is not uniform scaling. Convert units consistently: length, square-unit, and cubic-unit conversion factors differ.

references.title: Samples and statistical comparisons — quick reference
references.body:
## Sampling and inference

Define the target population before selecting a sample. A complete-roster simple random sample supports inference better than a convenience or voluntary-response group. Random selection does not guarantee perfect representation, and increasing the size of a biased sample does not remove its systematic selection problem.

Response is a separate stage. Report how many selected people answered, and do not count missing responses as known negative answers. For observed subgroup count $a$ among $n$ respondents, sample proportion is $a/n$. A matching population of size $N$ gives projected count $(a/n)N$. Label this as an estimate and state sampling limitations.

## Compare distributions

Mean is sum divided by count. Median is the middle of an ordered list, averaging the two middle values for even count. MAD is the mean of absolute distances from the mean. Compare center, spread, and overlap together. With similar variability, express a mean difference as a multiple of the common MAD for an informal descriptive comparison.

A larger sample generally gives less variable proportions under a comparable fair design, but not every larger sample is closer on every occasion. Sample size is observations per estimate; repetition count is how many estimates are generated. A simulation's observed minimum and maximum describe those runs and are not guaranteed future bounds.

Use comparable units, definitions, and time periods. Survey associations do not by themselves establish cause and effect.

references.title: Probability and simulation — quick reference
references.body:
## Build the probability model

Define basic outcomes, the sample space, and the event. Each probability lies from zero to one, and probabilities of disjoint exhaustive outcomes sum to one. Favorable count divided by total count requires equally likely counted outcomes. Distinct labels can group unequal numbers of basic outcomes.

The complement rule is $P(\text{not }A)=1-P(A)$. For compound events, use lists, tables, or trees to avoid omissions and double-counting. Multiply appropriate stage probabilities along a path. Independence must be justified; drawing without replacement changes later counter probabilities.

## Experiment and simulate

Relative frequency is successes divided by trials. Combine success counts and trial counts before dividing, especially when runs differ in size. Cumulative records already include earlier trials. Long-run relative frequency generally stabilizes under a stable independent model, but short-run results need not meet a quota and a streak does not make an independent outcome due.

A reproducible simulation states its random mapping, complete trial unit, success rule, dependency or replacement assumptions, and repetition procedure. Match the unit to the question: one visitor's success differs from an entire event exceeding its supply.

Expected count is probability times trials; it need not be an integer and is not a guaranteed count. Compare results with a theoretical calculation where possible, retain actual observed records, and label invented demonstrations. A model-based conclusion applies only under its stated assumptions.

drills.title: Add opposite signs
drills.prompt: Compute -{a} + {b}.
drills.solution: Cancel opposite amounts: the sum is {result}.

drills.title: Add two negative fractions
drills.prompt: Compute (-{a}/{d}) + (-{b}/{d}). Give an exact fraction.
drills.solution: Add the numerators and keep the negative direction: {result:frac}.

drills.title: Subtract a negative
drills.prompt: Compute {a} - (-{b}).
drills.solution: Add the inverse of -{b}: {a}+{b}={result}.

drills.title: Distance across zero
drills.prompt: Find the distance between -{a} and {b}. Give only the number of units.
drills.solution: Travel {a} units to zero and {b} more units: {result}.

drills.title: Negative times negative
drills.prompt: Compute (-{a})(-{b}).
drills.solution: Equal nonzero signs give a positive product: {result}.

drills.title: Signed quotient
drills.prompt: Compute -{total} ÷ {b}.
drills.solution: {b} times -{a} is -{total}, so the quotient is {result}.

drills.title: Fractions with denominator twenty
drills.prompt: Write {a}/20 as an exact decimal.
drills.solution: Multiply numerator and denominator by five: {result}.
drills.topic: Fractions, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals

drills.title: Signed eighths
drills.prompt: Write -{a}/8 as an exact decimal.
drills.solution: Divide the magnitude by eight, then restore the negative sign: {result}.
drills.topic: Fractions, terminating decimals, and repeating decimals

drills.title: Fractional-time speed
drills.prompt: A walker covers {a}/2 kilometers in 1/{b} hour. Find kilometers per hour.
drills.solution: Divide distance by time: ({a}/2) × {b} = {result:frac}.

drills.title: Price per kilogram
drills.prompt: A {a}/4-kilogram package costs {cost} dollars. Find dollars per kilogram.
drills.solution: Divide {cost} by {a}/4 to obtain {result} dollars per kilogram.

drills.title: Find the proportionality constant
drills.prompt: A proportional relationship contains x={x}, y={y}. Find y/x.
drills.solution: Divide {y} by {x}: the constant is {result}.

drills.title: Predict a proportional output
drills.prompt: A proportional rule has y={k}x. Find y when x={x}.
drills.solution: Multiply the input by the constant: {result}.

drills.title: Read a proportional output
drills.prompt: For y={k}x, find y when x={x}.
drills.solution: Substitute the input: y={k}×{x}={result}.

drills.title: Recover the input
drills.prompt: A proportional model is y={k}x. Find x when y={y}.
drills.solution: Divide the output by {k}: x={result}.

drills.title: Drawing to actual length
drills.prompt: A drawing uses 1 centimeter for {k} meters. A segment is {d} centimeters. Find its actual length in meters.
drills.solution: Multiply drawing length by the scale: {result} meters.

drills.title: Scale a rectangle area
drills.prompt: A rectangle drawing is {a} cm by {b} cm. Each centimeter represents {k} meters. Find actual area in square meters.
drills.solution: Both side lengths scale by {k}, so area is {a}×{b}×{k}×{k}={result}.

drills.title: Percent increase from a change
drills.prompt: An original amount is {base}. It increases by {change}. Find the percent increase as a number.
drills.solution: Divide {change} by {base} and multiply by 100: {result} percent.

drills.title: Percent error
drills.prompt: The accepted value is {base}; an estimate is {estimate}. Give the percent error as a number.
drills.solution: Use the absolute discrepancy divided by {base}: {result} percent.

drills.title: Discounted price
drills.prompt: A price is {price} dollars. Apply a {percent}% discount. Find the sale price in dollars.
drills.solution: Keep 100 minus {percent} percent of {price}: {result} dollars.

drills.title: Taxed price
drills.prompt: A taxable price is {price} dollars. The stated tax rate is {r}%. Find the total in dollars.
drills.solution: Add {r}% of {price}: the total is {result} dollars.

drills.title: Annual simple interest
drills.prompt: Find simple interest on {principal} dollars at {r}% annually for {t} years.
drills.solution: Use I=Prt: {principal}×({r}/100)×{t}={result} dollars.

drills.title: Tip on a stated subtotal
drills.prompt: A subtotal is {subtotal} dollars. Find a {percent}% tip on that subtotal.
drills.solution: Multiply the stated subtotal by the decimal tip rate: {result} dollars.

drills.title: Recover original after discount
drills.prompt: After a 25% discount, a price is {sale} dollars. Find the original price in dollars.
drills.solution: The sale is 75% of the original. Divide {sale} by 0.75 to get {result}.
drills.topic: Find an original amount and compare percent changes

drills.title: Recover original after increase
drills.prompt: After a 20% increase, an amount is {newAmount}. Find its original value.
drills.solution: Divide the new amount by 1.20: {result}.
drills.topic: Find an original amount and compare percent changes

drills.title: Combine integer coefficients
drills.prompt: Simplify {a}x - {b}x. Give only the coefficient of x.
drills.solution: Subtract coefficients of like terms: {result}.

drills.title: Combine fractional coefficients
drills.prompt: Simplify ({a}/{d})x + ({b}/{d})x. Give only the exact coefficient of x.
drills.solution: Use the common denominator and add numerators: {result:frac}.

drills.title: Expand and find the coefficient
drills.prompt: Expand {a}({b}x + {c}). Give only the coefficient of x.
drills.solution: Multiply the outside factor by the x coefficient: {result}.

drills.title: Distribute a negative factor
drills.prompt: Expand -{a}({b}x - {c}). Give only the constant term, including its sign.
drills.solution: Negative {a} times negative {c} is positive {result}.

drills.title: Repeated package cost
drills.prompt: There are {n} packages, each costing x dollars plus {fee} dollars. After expansion, give the fixed term in the total.
drills.solution: Each of {n} packages includes {fee}, so the fixed term is {result}.

drills.title: Percent multiplier
drills.prompt: An amount increases by {percent}%. Give the resulting multiplier as a decimal.
drills.solution: Add the decimal rate to one: {result}.

drills.title: Repeated grouped cost
drills.prompt: Each of {n} groups buys {a} items at {p} dollars each plus one {fee}-dollar item. Find the total cost.
drills.solution: One group pays {a}×{p}+{fee}. Multiply that complete amount by {n}: {result} dollars.

drills.title: Balance after signed changes
drills.prompt: A container starts with {start} liters, loses {loss} liters, then gains {gain} liters. Find the final amount.
drills.solution: Apply the changes to the starting amount: {start}−{loss}+{gain}={result} liters.

drills.title: Solve a two-step equation
drills.prompt: Solve {a}x + {b} = {rhs}. Give x.
drills.solution: Subtract {b}, then divide by {a}: x={result}.

drills.title: Solve with a negative coefficient
drills.prompt: Solve -{a}x + {b} = {rhs}. Give x.
drills.solution: Subtract {b}, then divide by -{a}: x={result}.

drills.title: Solve a grouped sum
drills.prompt: Solve {a}(x + {b}) = {rhs}. Give x.
drills.solution: Divide by {a}, then subtract {b}: x={result}.

drills.title: Solve a grouped difference
drills.prompt: Solve -{a}(x - {b}) = {rhs}. Give x.
drills.solution: Divide by -{a}, then add {b}: x={result}.

drills.title: Negative coefficient boundary
drills.prompt: Solve -{a}x < {rhs}. The solution is x > ___. Give the boundary number.
drills.solution: Divide by -{a} and reverse the sign: x>{result}.

drills.title: Positive coefficient boundary
drills.prompt: Solve {a}x + {b} ≤ {rhs}. The solution is x ≤ ___. Give the boundary number.
drills.solution: Subtract {b}, then divide by positive {a}: x≤{result}.

drills.title: Budget maximum
drills.prompt: A budget is {budget} dollars. A fixed fee is {fee} dollars and each item costs {cost} dollars. Find the maximum whole item count.
drills.solution: Subtract {fee}, then divide by {cost}: exactly {result} items fit.

drills.title: Minimum packages with a shortage
drills.prompt: Each package holds {size} items. You need {need} items. Find the minimum whole package count.
drills.solution: {n} packages provide one item too few, so buy {result} packages.

drills.title: Supplementary angle
drills.prompt: An angle measures {a} degrees. Find its supplement in degrees.
drills.solution: Subtract from 180: {result} degrees.

drills.title: Complementary angle
drills.prompt: An angle measures {a} degrees. Find its complement in degrees.
drills.solution: Subtract from 90: {result} degrees.

drills.title: Third triangle angle
drills.prompt: Two triangle angles measure {a} and {b} degrees. Find the third angle.
drills.solution: Subtract the two known angles from 180: {result} degrees.

drills.title: Largest integer third side
drills.prompt: Two sides have lengths {a} and {b}. Find the largest integer third-side length that can form a triangle.
drills.solution: The third side must be strictly less than {a}+{b}, so the largest integer is {result}.

drills.title: Area coefficient
drills.prompt: A circle has radius {r}. Its exact area is ___ times pi. Give the coefficient.
drills.solution: Square the radius: {result}. The area is {result}π square units.

drills.title: Circumference coefficient
drills.prompt: A circle has radius {r}. Its exact circumference is ___ times pi. Give the coefficient.
drills.solution: Double the radius: {result}. The circumference is {result}π units.

drills.title: Rectangle with corner cutout
drills.prompt: A {w}-by-{h} rectangle loses a {a}-by-{b} corner. Find remaining area.
drills.solution: Subtract the cutout area from the full rectangle: {result} square units.
drills.topic: Area and perimeter of composite figures

drills.title: Shared-edge perimeter
drills.prompt: Two regions have perimeters {p} and {q} and share exactly one edge of length {s}. Find their combined exterior perimeter.
drills.solution: Remove the shared edge from both individual counts: {result} units.
drills.topic: Area and perimeter of composite figures

drills.title: Prism section area
drills.prompt: A rectangular prism has a {a}-by-{b} base. An interior cut parallel to that base has what area?
drills.solution: The section matches the base: area={a}×{b}={result}.

drills.title: Prism section perimeter
drills.prompt: A rectangular prism is cut parallel to a {a}-by-{b} face. Find the section perimeter.
drills.solution: The rectangular section has perimeter 2({a}+{b})={result}.

drills.title: Rectangular-prism volume
drills.prompt: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism measuring {a} by {b} by {h}.
drills.solution: Base area times height gives {result} cubic units.

drills.title: Triangular-prism volume
drills.prompt: A triangular base has base edge {b} and perpendicular altitude {a}. The right prism extends {h} units. Find volume.
drills.solution: Use half the triangle base times altitude, then multiply by prism length: {result:frac}.

drills.title: Closed rectangular-box area
drills.prompt: Find the total surface area of a closed {a}-by-{b}-by-{h} rectangular box.
drills.solution: Count two faces of each size: {result} square units.
drills.topic: Use nets to find surface area

drills.title: Cube surface area
drills.prompt: A cube has side length {s}. Find its total surface area.
drills.solution: Six square faces each have area {s}²: total {result}.
drills.topic: Use nets to find surface area

drills.title: Stacked-prism volume
drills.prompt: A lower prism is {a} by {b} by {h}. An upper prism on it is {c} by {b} by {k}, with no interior overlap. Find total volume.
drills.solution: Add the lower and upper volumes: {result} cubic units.
drills.topic: Measure composite solids and scale effects

drills.title: Uniform volume scale
drills.prompt: A solid has volume {v}. Every length is multiplied by {s}. Find the new volume.
drills.solution: Multiply by the cube of {s}: the new volume is {result}.
drills.topic: Measure composite solids and scale effects

drills.title: Fraction sampled
drills.prompt: A population has {total} members. A random sample contains {sample} members. Give the sampled fraction exactly.
drills.solution: Divide sample size by population size: {sample}/{total}={result:frac}.

drills.title: Response count
drills.prompt: A random sample of {selected} people is selected. Exactly {missing} do not respond. How many respond?
drills.solution: Subtract nonrespondents from selected people: {result}.

drills.title: Project a sample proportion
drills.prompt: A representative random sample has {yesCount} people with a feature out of {sample}. Estimate the count in a population of {population}.
drills.solution: Apply {yesCount}/20 to {population}: about {result} people.
drills.topic: Use samples to estimate population quantities

drills.title: Respondent percent
drills.prompt: Exactly {yesCount} of {sample} respondents choose an option. Give the observed percent as a number.
drills.solution: Divide {yesCount} by 40 and multiply by 100: {result} percent.
drills.topic: Use samples to estimate population quantities

drills.title: Mean of symmetric data
drills.prompt: Find the mean of {lo}, {c}, {c}, {hi}.
drills.solution: The values balance around {c}, and their sum divided by four is {result}.

drills.title: MAD of symmetric data
drills.prompt: Find the MAD of {lo}, {c}, {c}, {hi}. The mean is {c}.
drills.solution: Distances are {d}, 0, 0, {d}; their mean is {result:frac}.

drills.title: Sample percentage
drills.prompt: A simulated sample has {success} successes out of {total} trials. Give the sample percent as a number.
drills.solution: Divide by twenty and multiply by one hundred: {result} percent.

drills.title: Total simulation draws
drills.prompt: A simulation uses {runs} repeated samples, each with {size} draws. How many draws altogether?
drills.solution: Multiply repetitions by observations per sample: {result}.

drills.title: Counter probability
drills.prompt: A bag has {a} red and {b} blue counters, each equally likely. Find P(red) as an exact fraction.
drills.solution: Use red count divided by total count: {result:frac}.

drills.title: Complement probability
drills.prompt: An event has probability {a}/20. Find the probability of its complement as an exact fraction.
drills.solution: Subtract from one: (20−{a})/20={result:frac}.

drills.title: Experimental percent
drills.prompt: An event occurs {success} times in {trials} trials. Give its experimental probability as a percent number.
drills.solution: Divide {success} by 40, then multiply by 100: {result} percent.

drills.title: Predicted future count
drills.prompt: An experimental estimate is {a}/20. Use it to predict the number of successes in {trials} future trials.
drills.solution: Multiply the estimated probability by the future trial count: about {result} successes.

drills.title: Two-stage combination count
drills.prompt: A first stage has {a} choices and each leads to {b} second-stage choices. How many ordered combinations exist?
drills.solution: Count {b} continuations for each of {a} starts: {result}.

drills.title: Two draws with replacement
drills.prompt: A bag has {a} red and {b} blue counters, equally likely individually. Draw twice with replacement and mixing. Find P(red both times).
drills.solution: The red probability stays {a}/({a}+{b}); square it: {result:frac}.

drills.title: Simulated success percentage
drills.prompt: A complete trial has two draws. In {trials} complete trials, {wins} meet the success rule. Give the experimental success percent.
drills.solution: Divide successful complete trials by all complete trials: {result} percent.
drills.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model

drills.title: Expected count from a model
drills.prompt: A modeled event has probability {a}/16. For {trials} independent complete trials, find the expected count.
drills.solution: Probability times trial count gives an expected {result}, not a guaranteed observed count.
drills.topic: Design simulations and evaluate a complete model
